SQL

Chapters 6, 7.1, 7.3, 7.4, 10.1 & 10.2 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 6.5–6.13, 6.15, 7.1–7.9, 10.7. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

SQL is declarative like the calculus, with algebra-like operators underneath and practical additions: NULLs, grouping, views. Every query here was run on the COMPANY and UNIVERSITY data, so the result tables are real output. Read a query in its logical order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY); most of the classic traps come from reading it in written order.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  SQL at a glance

    Theory recap

    SQL (Structured Query Language, originally SEQUEL, from IBM’s SYSTEM R) is the standard relational language. It is declarative: you say what result you want, the DBMS decides how. It is based more on tuple relational calculus than on relational algebra. One language covers DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP), DML (SELECT/INSERT/DELETE/UPDATE), constraints, views, and (in later chapters) triggers, transactions and authorization.

    Formal model (Ch 5)SQL termDifference
    relationtablea table is a multiset (bag) of rows unless a key or DISTINCT makes it a set
    tuplerowrows are unordered; columns are ordered (in CREATE TABLE order)
    attributecolumna column may be NULL unless declared NOT NULL

    The six clauses and the order in which they are evaluated

    A query has up to six clauses; only SELECT and FROM are required.

    General form of a retrieval query
    SELECT   <attribute and function list>      -- 5. pick / compute output columns
FROM     <table list>                       -- 1. form the tuple combinations (joins)
[WHERE   <condition>]                       -- 2. keep rows where condition is TRUE
[GROUP BY <grouping attributes>]            -- 3. partition rows into groups
[HAVING  <group condition>]                 -- 4. keep groups where condition is TRUE
[ORDER BY <attribute list> [ASC|DESC]];     -- 6. sort the final result
    Logical (conceptual) evaluation order

    FROM →\rightarrow→ WHERE →\rightarrow→ GROUP BY →\rightarrow→ HAVING →\rightarrow→ SELECT (then DISTINCT) →\rightarrow→ ORDER BY. The writing order is different from the evaluation order. Consequences you are tested on:

    • WHERE cannot use an aggregate (groups do not exist yet). Use HAVING for conditions on COUNT, SUM, …
    • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.
    • A column alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE (SELECT runs later); standard SQL allows it in ORDER BY.
    • With GROUP BY, every SELECT column that is not inside an aggregate must be a grouping column.
    • ORDER BY is the only thing that guarantees an order; a table (and a result) has no order otherwise.

    The real execution plan is chosen by the optimizer (footnote in §7.1.11); this order only defines the meaning.

    How SQL answers are graded (from the IA6 and GA6 keys and rubrics)
    • Assumptions earn marks (IA6: 1 mark in every part). Write them as SQL comments (– Assumption: ISBN is the key of BOOKS, so COUNT(*) counts books). Full mark only if the reason or effect is given; half if just stated. Typical ones: which attributes are keys, that key/FK columns are never NULL (needed for NOT IN), how ties are handled, whether empty groups (a publisher with no books, a book with no co-authors) must appear.
    • Any dialect is fine (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle, standard). Small syntax slips (a missing comma or semicolon, keyword case) cost nothing unless they change the result.
    • Many correct answers: joins, IN, EXISTS, EXCEPT, WITH, window functions are all accepted. The marker checks whether the right rows come back.
    • Typical deductions: ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 when ties are possible (lost 2.5/10 in IA6(b)); an inner join that drops rows with no match, e.g. books with no co-authors (−1-1−1); 1 + COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN (counts the NULL-padded row); grouping by the wrong attribute (by Title instead of ISBN; by one column instead of two); ORDER BY keys in the wrong order or missing DESC (ascending is the default); OR instead of AND for “neither … nor” (lost the whole combine criterion); a join on <> to express “not related” (almost everything is returned); NOT IN on a column that may contain NULL without an assumption.
    • Procedural questions (GA6, SQL for each step of an algorithm): give an SQL statement per step; conditions must be checked on the current (reduced) table, not the original; return a list with ORDER BY on a position column, because a table has no order. A worked trace must match what your own SQL returns (error carried forward is not penalised twice).
    • Bare answers: in “write the output” or “trace” parts, a correct result with no working gets only the final-answer mark. Show the intermediate table (joined rows, groups) first.

    3  Data definition and constraints · §6.1–6.2

    Theory recap

    Schemas and catalogs

    An SQL schema groups the tables, types, domains, views, constraints and grants of one application; it has a name and an authorization identifier (owner): CREATE SCHEMA COMPANY AUTHORIZATION ’Jsmith’;. A catalog is a named collection of schemas and always contains INFORMATION_SCHEMA (descriptions of all schemas). Referential integrity can be declared only between relations in the same catalog.

    CREATE TABLE

    CREATE TABLE [schema.]name (col type [col constraints], …, [table constraints]); creates a base table (stored as a file), in contrast to a view (virtual). Columns are ordered as declared; rows are not ordered.

    Type familySQL types (§6.1.3)
    NumericINTEGER/INT, SMALLINT; FLOAT/REAL, DOUBLE PRECISION; DECIMAL(i,j) = DEC/NUMERIC: precision iii = total digits, scale jjj = digits after the point (default scale 0)
    Character stringCHAR(n) fixed (padded with blanks), VARCHAR(n) varying (max nnn); CLOB(20M); literals in single quotes, case sensitive; concatenation ||
    Bit stringBIT(n), BIT VARYING(n), BLOB(30G); literal B’10101’
    BooleanTRUE, FALSE (and UNKNOWN because of NULL)
    Date/timeDATE (YYYY-MM-DD), TIME (HH:MM:SS), TIME(i), TIME WITH TIME ZONE, TIMESTAMP, INTERVAL; literals DATE ’2014-09-27’

    A domain names a type (with optional default and CHECK) so it can be reused and changed in one place: CREATE DOMAIN SSN_TYPE AS CHAR(9); CREATE DOMAIN D_NUM AS INTEGER CHECK (D_NUM > 0 AND D_NUM < 21);

    Constraints

    ConstraintMeaning and syntax
    NOT NULLcolumn may not be NULL. Implied for primary-key columns.
    DEFAULT vvalue used when an INSERT omits the column. With no DEFAULT the “default default” is NULL.
    CHECK (cond) on a column/domainrestricts values: Dnumber INT NOT NULL CHECK (Dnumber > 0 AND Dnumber < 21)
    PRIMARY KEY (A,…)entity integrity + uniqueness; one per table. Single-column form: Dnumber INT PRIMARY KEY
    UNIQUE (A,…)alternate (candidate) key: UNIQUE (Dname)
    FOREIGN KEY (A) REFERENCES T(K)referential integrity, with optional triggered actions (below)
    CONSTRAINT name …names a constraint so it can later be dropped/replaced with ALTER TABLE; names unique in the schema
    tuple-level CHECKat the end of CREATE TABLE, checked for each inserted/modified row: CHECK (Dept_create_date <= Mgr_start_date)
    Definition: Referential triggered actions

    The default reaction to an operation that would violate a foreign key is to reject it (RESTRICT / NO ACTION). The designer may instead attach ON DELETE and/or ON UPDATE with one of:

    • SET NULL: the referencing FK values become NULL (impossible if the FK column is NOT NULL or part of the PK);
    • SET DEFAULT: they become the column’s DEFAULT (which must itself be a valid reference);
    • CASCADE: ON DELETE deletes the referencing rows; ON UPDATE copies the new key value into them.

    These fire when a referenced (parent) row is deleted or its key is updated. Inserting a child row with a non-existent FK value, or updating a child’s FK to one, is always rejected.

    Which action to choose (book’s rule of thumb, §6.2.2)

    CASCADE suits relations that cannot exist without the parent: relationship relations (WORKS_ON), multivalued-attribute relations (DEPT_LOCATIONS), weak entities (DEPENDENT). SET NULL suits optional links (Super_ssn: an employee survives the loss of the supervisor). SET DEFAULT when a sensible default exists (new department 1). RESTRICT when deleting the parent would lose important information (do not delete a borrower with books out). ON UPDATE CASCADE is almost always right: a corrected key should follow everywhere.

    The COMPANY DDL (Figures 6.1 and 6.2 combined)

    COMPANY schema with defaults / named constraints and triggered actions
    CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE
( Fname      VARCHAR(15)    NOT NULL,
  Minit      CHAR,
  Lname      VARCHAR(15)    NOT NULL,
  Ssn        CHAR(9)        NOT NULL,
  Bdate      DATE,
  Address    VARCHAR(30),
  Sex        CHAR,
  Salary     DECIMAL(10,2),
  Super_ssn  CHAR(9),
  Dno        INT            NOT NULL  DEFAULT 1,
  CONSTRAINT EMPPK      PRIMARY KEY (Ssn),
  CONSTRAINT EMPSUPERFK FOREIGN KEY (Super_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn)
                        ON DELETE SET NULL      ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT EMPDEPTFK  FOREIGN KEY (Dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(Dnumber)
                        ON DELETE SET DEFAULT   ON UPDATE CASCADE );
CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT
( Dname          VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,
  Dnumber        INT          NOT NULL,
  Mgr_ssn        CHAR(9)      NOT NULL  DEFAULT '888665555',
  Mgr_start_date DATE,
  CONSTRAINT DEPTPK    PRIMARY KEY (Dnumber),
  CONSTRAINT DEPTSK    UNIQUE (Dname),
  CONSTRAINT DEPTMGRFK FOREIGN KEY (Mgr_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn)
                       ON DELETE SET DEFAULT   ON UPDATE CASCADE );
CREATE TABLE DEPT_LOCATIONS
( Dnumber    INT          NOT NULL,
  Dlocation  VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Dnumber, Dlocation),
  FOREIGN KEY (Dnumber) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(Dnumber)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE );
CREATE TABLE PROJECT
( Pname      VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,
  Pnumber    INT          NOT NULL,
  Plocation  VARCHAR(15),
  Dnum       INT          NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Pnumber),
  UNIQUE (Pname),
  FOREIGN KEY (Dnum) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(Dnumber) );
CREATE TABLE WORKS_ON
( Essn   CHAR(9)       NOT NULL,
  Pno    INT           NOT NULL,
  Hours  DECIMAL(3,1)  NOT NULL,      -- Figure 6.1 says NOT NULL, yet Fig 5.6 has a NULL
  PRIMARY KEY (Essn, Pno),
  FOREIGN KEY (Essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn),
  FOREIGN KEY (Pno)  REFERENCES PROJECT(Pnumber) );
CREATE TABLE DEPENDENT
( Essn            CHAR(9)      NOT NULL,
  Dependent_name  VARCHAR(15)  NOT NULL,
  Sex             CHAR,
  Bdate           DATE,
  Relationship    VARCHAR(8),
  PRIMARY KEY (Essn, Dependent_name),
  FOREIGN KEY (Essn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn) );
    Circular and forward references

    EMPLOYEE.Dno refers to DEPARTMENT, which is not created yet, and DEPARTMENT.Mgr_ssn refers back to EMPLOYEE; Super_ssn is a self-reference. In a real DBMS create the tables without those FKs and add them afterwards with ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT … (§13). The same cycle means the first rows must be loaded with checks deferred (or with the FK added after loading).

    Worked example: CREATE TABLE with types, CHECK, DEFAULT and ON DELETE (past-paper pattern)

    Hospital: doctors, patients and admissions. Fee non-negative; specialty defaults to ‘General’; an admission’s status is Admitted or Discharged (default Admitted); discharge not before admission; deleting a patient removes their admissions; deleting a doctor keeps the admission but forgets the doctor.

    CREATE TABLE DOCTOR
( Doc_id     INT           PRIMARY KEY,
  Name       VARCHAR(30)   NOT NULL,
  Specialty  VARCHAR(20)   DEFAULT 'General',
  Fee        DECIMAL(8,2)  NOT NULL CHECK (Fee >= 0) );
CREATE TABLE PATIENT
( Pat_id     INT           PRIMARY KEY,
  Name       VARCHAR(30)   NOT NULL,
  Sex        CHAR(1)       CHECK (Sex IN ('M','F','O')),
  Age        INT           CHECK (Age BETWEEN 0 AND 130) );
CREATE TABLE ADMISSION
( Adm_id     INT           PRIMARY KEY,
  Pat_id     INT           NOT NULL,          -- every admission has a patient
  Doc_id     INT,                             -- nullable: needed for SET NULL
  Adm_date   DATE          NOT NULL,
  Dis_date   DATE,                            -- NULL while still admitted
  Status     VARCHAR(10)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Admitted'
                           CHECK (Status IN ('Admitted','Discharged')),
  Bill       DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 0 CHECK (Bill >= 0),
  CONSTRAINT ADM_DATES CHECK (Dis_date IS NULL OR Dis_date >= Adm_date),  -- tuple CHECK
  CONSTRAINT ADM_PAT FOREIGN KEY (Pat_id) REFERENCES PATIENT(Pat_id)
                     ON DELETE CASCADE  ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT ADM_DOC FOREIGN KEY (Doc_id) REFERENCES DOCTOR(Doc_id)
                     ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE );

    Checked in SQLite: INSERT INTO DOCTOR (Doc_id, Name, Fee) VALUES (1,’Rao’,500) stores Specialty = ‘General’; a negative fee, a discharge date before the admission date and an admission for a non-existent patient are all rejected; deleting doctor 1 sets Doc_id to NULL in that doctor’s admissions; deleting a patient deletes their admissions. Doc_id must be nullable because SET NULL on a NOT NULL column can never succeed.

    4  Basic retrieval queries · §6.3

    Theory recap

    SELECT–FROM–WHERE

    SELECT lists the output attributes (the projection), FROM the tables, WHERE a Boolean condition combining selection conditions and join conditions. Conceptually: for each combination of one row from each FROM table, evaluate WHERE; if TRUE, output the SELECT values.

    Q0, Q1, Q2 on Figure 5.6
    -- Q0: birth date and address of John B. Smith          (select-project)
SELECT Bdate, Address FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Fname = 'John' AND Minit = 'B' AND Lname = 'Smith';
-- Q1: name and address of employees in 'Research'       (select-project-join)
SELECT Fname, Lname, Address FROM EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT
WHERE  Dname = 'Research' AND Dnumber = Dno;
-- Q2: projects located in Stafford: number, dept, manager's name, address, bdate
SELECT Pnumber, Dnum, Lname, Address, Bdate
FROM   PROJECT, DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Dnum = Dnumber AND Mgr_ssn = Ssn AND Plocation = 'Stafford';

    Results: Q0 →\to→ (1965-01-09, 731 Fondren, Houston, TX). Q1 →\to→ Smith, Wong, Narayan, English. Q2 →\to→ (10, 4, Wallace, 291 Berry, Bellaire, TX, 1941-06-20) and (30, 4, Wallace, …).

    Ambiguous names, aliases and tuple variables

    If two tables have a column with the same name, qualify it: EMPLOYEE.Dno. When the same table appears twice (a recursive relationship), you must declare aliases (tuple variables):

    Q8: each employee with his or her immediate supervisor
    SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname, S.Fname, S.Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E, EMPLOYEE AS S          -- AS is optional
WHERE  E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn;

    Result: 7 rows (everyone except Borg, whose Super_ssn is NULL and matches nothing). Attributes can be renamed in FROM too: EMPLOYEE AS E(Fn, Mi, Ln, Ssn, Bd, Addr, Sex, Sal, Sssn, Dno).

    Missing WHERE, the asterisk

    No WHERE = every row qualifies. Several tables and no WHERE = Cartesian product: SELECT Ssn, Dname FROM EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT gives 8×3=248 \times 3 = 248×3=24 rows. Forgetting a join condition produces this inflated result. SELECT * returns all columns; E.* all columns of one table.

    Tables as multisets: DISTINCT and set operations

    SQL does not remove duplicates automatically because (1) it is expensive (sort/hash), (2) the user may want them, (3) aggregates usually need them (an AVG over salaries must count 25000 three times). SELECT ALL (the default) keeps duplicates; SELECT DISTINCT removes them. SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE gives 8 values; SELECT DISTINCT Salary gives 6.

    UNION, EXCEPT (Oracle: MINUS) and INTERSECT need type-compatible operands (same number of columns, compatible types, same order) and return sets (duplicates removed). UNION ALL, EXCEPT ALL, INTERSECT ALL are the multiset versions: each copy is treated as a separate element.

    Figure 6.5: multiset operations on R(A) = {a1, a2, a2, a3}, S(A) = {a1, a2, a4, a5}
    R UNION ALL S= {a1, a1, a2, a2, a2, a3, a4, a5}(8 rows: counts add)
    R EXCEPT ALL S= {a2, a3}(count = max⁡(0,m−n)\max(0, m-n)max(0,m−n): a2 is 2 in R, 1 in S)
    R INTERSECT ALL S= {a1, a2}(count = min⁡(m,n)\min(m,n)min(m,n))
    R UNION S= {a1, a2, a3, a4, a5}(set: duplicates removed)
    Q4: projects involving a ’Smith’ as worker or as manager of the controlling department
    (SELECT DISTINCT Pnumber
 FROM   PROJECT, DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
 WHERE  Dnum = Dnumber AND Mgr_ssn = Ssn AND Lname = 'Smith')
UNION
(SELECT DISTINCT Pnumber
 FROM   PROJECT, WORKS_ON, EMPLOYEE
 WHERE  Pnumber = Pno AND Essn = Ssn AND Lname = 'Smith');    -- result: 1, 2

    LIKE, arithmetic, BETWEEN, ORDER BY

    • LIKE: % = any string of 0 or more characters, _ = exactly one character; ESCAPE ’\’ for literal % or _; an apostrophe inside a string is written twice (”).
    • Arithmetic + - * / on numbers, || on strings, date ±\pm± interval; rename computed columns with AS.
    • x BETWEEN a AND b ≡\equiv≡ x >= a AND x <= b (inclusive).
    • ORDER BY c1 [ASC|DESC], c2 …: ascending by default; ties on c1 are broken by c2.
    SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Address LIKE 'SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Bdate LIKE '__5_______';           -- Q12A: born 195x
SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname, 1.1 * E.Salary AS Increased_sal                   -- Q13
FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E, WORKS_ON AS W, PROJECT AS P
WHERE  E.Ssn = W.Essn AND W.Pno = P.Pnumber AND P.Pname = 'ProductX';
SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE (Salary BETWEEN 30000 AND 40000) AND Dno = 5; -- Q14
SELECT D.Dname, E.Lname, E.Fname, P.Pname                                  -- Q15
FROM   DEPARTMENT D, EMPLOYEE E, WORKS_ON W, PROJECT P
WHERE  D.Dnumber = E.Dno AND E.Ssn = W.Essn AND W.Pno = P.Pnumber
ORDER BY D.Dname DESC, E.Lname ASC, E.Fname ASC;

    Results: Q12 →\to→ Smith, Wong, English, Jabbar, Borg. Q12A →\to→ Wong (1955). Q13 →\to→ Smith 33000, English 27500. Q14 →\to→ Smith, Wong, Narayan (both ends included).

    Exact strings

    The book prints Q12 as ’%Houston,TX%’ (no space), which matches no row of Figure 5.6 because the addresses contain “Houston, TX”. String literals are compared exactly (and case-sensitively). Q12A’s text says “1950s” but its pattern has a 7 (1970s); the pattern ’__5_______’ is the 1950s one.

    5  INSERT, DELETE, UPDATE · §6.4

    Theory recap
    -- U1: full row, values in CREATE TABLE column order
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE VALUES ('Richard','K','Marini','653298653','1962-12-30',
       '98 Oak Forest, Katy, TX','M',37000,'653298653',4);
-- U1A: named columns; omitted columns get DEFAULT or NULL
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (Fname, Lname, Dno, Ssn) VALUES ('Richard','Marini',4,'653298653');
-- U3B: insert the result of a query (a snapshot: NOT kept up to date, unlike a view)
INSERT INTO WORKS_ON_INFO (Emp_name, Proj_name, Hours_per_week)
SELECT E.Lname, P.Pname, W.Hours
FROM   PROJECT P, WORKS_ON W, EMPLOYEE E
WHERE  P.Pnumber = W.Pno AND W.Essn = E.Ssn;
-- copy structure and data
CREATE TABLE D5EMPS LIKE EMPLOYEE (SELECT E.* FROM EMPLOYEE AS E WHERE E.Dno = 5) WITH DATA;
-- U4A-U4D: delete 0, 1, 4, all rows of Figure 5.6 respectively
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Lname = 'Brown';
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Ssn = '123456789';
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = 5;
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE;                          -- table stays, empty (DROP TABLE removes it)
-- U5, U6
UPDATE PROJECT  SET Plocation = 'Bellaire', Dnum = 5 WHERE Pnumber = 10;
UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Salary = Salary * 1.1 WHERE Dno = 5;   -- right side = old value
    • INSERT must supply every NOT NULL column without a default. The DBMS rejects violations: U2 (Dno = 2, no such department) breaks referential integrity; U2A (no Ssn) breaks entity integrity.
    • DELETE and UPDATE act on one table at a time; effects spread to other tables only through referential triggered actions. SET can assign NULL or DEFAULT.
    • The WHERE of DELETE/UPDATE may contain nested queries (e.g. WHERE Dno IN (SELECT Dnumber FROM DEPARTMENT WHERE Dname = ’Research’)).

    6  NULL and three-valued logic · §7.1.1

    Theory recap

    NULL means unknown, unavailable/withheld or not applicable; SQL does not distinguish them, and every NULL is treated as different from every other NULL. Any comparison involving NULL (=, <>, <, >, …) yields UNKNOWN.

    ANDTRUEFALSEUNKNOWN
    TRUETRUEFALSEUNKNOWN
    FALSEFALSEFALSEFALSE
    UNKNOWNUNKNOWNFALSEUNKNOWN

      

    ORTRUEFALSEUNKNOWN
    TRUETRUETRUETRUE
    FALSETRUEFALSEUNKNOWN
    UNKNOWNTRUEUNKNOWNUNKNOWN

      

    NOT
    TRUEFALSE
    FALSETRUE
    UNKNOWNUNKNOWN
    Rules to remember
    • WHERE and HAVING keep a row/group only if the condition is TRUE; FALSE and UNKNOWN are both dropped. So WHERE B <> ’y’ does not return rows with B NULL.
    • Test for NULL with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL (always UNKNOWN, returns nothing).
    • Join conditions never match on NULL (except that outer joins keep the unmatched row, padded with NULLs).
    • GROUP BY puts all NULLs of the grouping column in one group; DISTINCT likewise treats NULLs as duplicates.
    Q18: employees with no supervisor
    SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Super_ssn IS NULL;      -- James Borg
    NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns nothing

    v NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means v<>1 AND v<>2 AND v<>NULL; the last part is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition is never TRUE. Example (tables R, S of §8.2): SELECT A FROM R WHERE B NOT IN (SELECT B FROM S) returns no rows because S.B contains a NULL, while the NOT EXISTS version returns A = 1 and 3. Either state “the column is never NULL” as an assumption (IA6 does) or use NOT EXISTS / filter IS NOT NULL in the subquery.

    7  Nested queries · §7.1.2–7.1.5

    Theory recap

    A nested query (subquery) is a complete SELECT block inside WHERE (or FROM, SELECT, HAVING). The enclosing query is the outer query.

    OperatorTRUE when
    v IN (Q) / v = ANY (Q) / = SOMEvvv equals some value of Q (IN ≡\equiv≡ = ANY)
    v NOT IN (Q)vvv differs from every value of Q (beware NULLs)
    v op ANY (Q), op ∈{<,≤,>,≥,≠}\in\{<,\le,>,\ge,\ne\}∈{<,≤,>,≥,=}vvv op qqq for at least one qqq (FALSE if Q empty)
    v op ALL (Q)vvv op qqq for every qqq (TRUE if Q is empty)
    (a,b) IN (Q)tuple comparison with a two-column subquery
    EXISTS (Q) / NOT EXISTS (Q)Q returns at least one row / no rows
    UNIQUE (Q)Q has no duplicate rows
    v = (Q)Q returns a single value (scalar subquery)
    -- salary greater than everyone in department 5  (equivalently: > (SELECT MAX(Salary) ...))
SELECT Lname, Fname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = 5);       -- Wallace, Borg
-- same (project, hours) combination as some project of John Smith
SELECT DISTINCT Essn FROM WORKS_ON
WHERE  (Pno, Hours) IN (SELECT Pno, Hours FROM WORKS_ON WHERE Essn = '123456789');
                                                                      -- only 123456789 itself

    Scope rule: an unqualified attribute refers to the table of the innermost query that has it; to reach the outer table, qualify with its alias.

    Correlated nested queries

    A subquery is correlated when its WHERE refers to an attribute of the outer query; think of it as being re-evaluated for each outer row. Queries using nested blocks with = or IN can always be flattened into a single block with joins.

    Q16: employees with a dependent of the same first name and sex (three equivalent forms)
    SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname FROM EMPLOYEE AS E
WHERE  E.Ssn IN (SELECT D.Essn FROM DEPENDENT AS D
                 WHERE  E.Fname = D.Dependent_name AND E.Sex = D.Sex);
SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname FROM EMPLOYEE AS E, DEPENDENT AS D            -- Q16A
WHERE  E.Ssn = D.Essn AND E.Sex = D.Sex AND E.Fname = D.Dependent_name;
SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname FROM EMPLOYEE AS E                            -- Q16B
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT * FROM DEPENDENT AS D
               WHERE E.Ssn = D.Essn AND E.Sex = D.Sex AND E.Fname = D.Dependent_name);
-- result on Figure 5.6: empty (Fig. 6.4(c))
    -- Q6: employees with no dependents   -> Zelaya, Narayan, English, Jabbar, Borg
SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM DEPENDENT WHERE Ssn = Essn);
-- Q7: managers with at least one dependent   -> Wong, Wallace
SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT * FROM DEPENDENT  WHERE Ssn = Essn)
  AND  EXISTS (SELECT * FROM DEPARTMENT WHERE Ssn = Mgr_ssn);
-- Q5: employees with two or more dependents   -> Smith, Wong
SELECT Lname, Fname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM DEPENDENT WHERE Ssn = Essn) >= 2;

    “For all” (division) queries

    SQL has no universal quantifier. “Employees who work on all projects controlled by department ddd” is rewritten as “there is no project of ddd that the employee does not work on”.

    Q3A: set difference must be empty
    SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  NOT EXISTS ( (SELECT Pnumber FROM PROJECT WHERE Dnum = 5)
                    EXCEPT
                    (SELECT Pno FROM WORKS_ON WHERE Ssn = Essn) );
    Q3B: double NOT EXISTS
    SELECT Lname, Fname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM WORKS_ON B
                    WHERE  B.Pno IN (SELECT Pnumber FROM PROJECT WHERE Dnum = 5)
                      AND  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM WORKS_ON C
                                        WHERE  C.Essn = Ssn AND C.Pno = B.Pno ) );

    On Figure 5.6 both return no rows for department 5 (nobody works on all of projects 1, 2, 3). With Dnum = 4 (projects 10 and 30) both return Zelaya and Jabbar. Q3B scans WORKS_ON B for the department’s projects, so a project of ddd on which nobody works would not be checked; Q3A (which takes the projects from PROJECT) is the safer pattern. A third pattern compares counts: GROUP BY Essn HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT Pno) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PROJECT WHERE Dnum = 5) after restricting WORKS_ON to those projects.

    Explicit sets and renaming

    WHERE Pno IN (1, 2, 3) uses an explicit set (Q17: result 123456789, 333445555, 453453453, 666884444 with DISTINCT). AS renames output columns: SELECT E.Lname AS Employee_name, S.Lname AS Supervisor_name …

    8  Joined tables and outer joins · §7.1.6

    Theory recap

    A joined table in FROM separates join conditions from selection conditions: FROM (EMPLOYEE JOIN DEPARTMENT ON Dno = Dnumber) WHERE Dname = ’Research’.

    JoinRows returned
    [INNER] JOIN … ON conly pairs satisfying c (default join)
    NATURAL JOINimplicit equality on all same-named columns, each kept once (rename with AS DEPT(Dname, Dno, Mssn, Msdate) to control which columns match)
    LEFT [OUTER] JOINinner rows + every unmatched left row padded with NULLs
    RIGHT [OUTER] JOINinner rows + every unmatched right row padded with NULLs
    FULL [OUTER] JOINinner rows + unmatched rows of both sides
    CROSS JOINCartesian product (∣R∣×∣S∣|R|\times|S|∣R∣×∣S∣ rows)
    NATURAL LEFT OUTER JOIN etc.natural version of an outer join

    Joins can be nested (multiway join), e.g. Q2A: FROM ((PROJECT JOIN DEPARTMENT ON Dnum = Dnumber) JOIN EMPLOYEE ON Mgr_ssn = Ssn). Old Oracle syntax wrote outer joins as +=, =+, +=+ in WHERE.

    Q8B: every employee with the supervisor’s name / if any
    SELECT E.Lname AS Employee_name, S.Lname AS Supervisor_name
FROM   (EMPLOYEE AS E LEFT OUTER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS S ON E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn);
-- 8 rows; Borg appears with Supervisor_name = NULL (the inner join Q8A gives 7)

    Which Venn regions each join returns

    Think of the left table A and right table B as circles; the overlap is “rows with a match”.

    The “only A” region is the anti-join: rows of A with no match (LEFT JOIN … WHERE B.key IS NULL, where B.key is a column that is never NULL in B, e.g. its primary key). The last diagram is the symmetric difference.

    Worked example: writing the output of joins on small tables, with NULLs

    R(A, B) and S(B, C)
    R

    Step 1: inner join. Only y matches: rows 2 and 4 of R each pair with (y,10) and (y,20): 4 rows. The NULL in R.B and the NULL in S.B do not match each other (NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN).
    Step 2: left join adds the unmatched R rows (1, x, NULL, NULL) and (3, NULL, NULL, NULL): 4+2=64+2=64+2=6.
    Step 3: right join adds the unmatched S rows (NULL, NULL, z, 30) and (NULL, NULL, NULL, 40): 4+2=64+2=64+2=6.
    Step 4: full join = inner + unmatched left + unmatched right =4+2+2=8= 4+2+2 = 8=4+2+2=8.

    Tuple-count rule: ∣R⟗S∣=∣R⋈S∣+(#unmatched R)+(#unmatched S)|R \mathbin{\text{⟗}} S| = |R \mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{}}} S| + (\#\text{unmatched } R) + (\#\text{unmatched } S)∣R⟗S∣=∣R⋈​S∣+(#unmatched R)+(#unmatched S), and ∣R⟕S∣=∣R⋈S∣+#unmatched R ≥∣R∣|R \mathbin{\text{⟕}} S| = |R \mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{}}} S| + \#\text{unmatched } R \ \ge |R|∣R⟕S∣=∣R⋈​S∣+#unmatched R ≥∣R∣. Count the inner join first, then add the padded rows.

    Group the left join:

    SELECT R.B, COUNT(*), COUNT(S.C), SUM(S.C)
FROM   R LEFT JOIN S ON R.B = S.B
GROUP BY R.B
HAVING COUNT(S.C) > 0;            -- remove this line to see all three groups
    R.BCOUNT(*)COUNT(S.C)SUM(S.C)
    NULL10NULL

     →HAVING COUNT(S.C)>0\xrightarrow{\text{HAVING COUNT(S.C)} > 0}HAVING COUNT(S.C)>0​ 

    R.BCOUNT(*)COUNT(S.C)SUM(S.C)

    The NULL values of R.B form one group; COUNT(*) counts the NULL-padded row (1) while COUNT(S.C) does not (0); SUM over no values is NULL, not 0.

    Building a FULL OUTER JOIN from other joins

    If the DBMS lacks FULL JOIN (older MySQL):

    SELECT R.A, R.B, S.B, S.C FROM R LEFT  JOIN S ON R.B = S.B
UNION
SELECT R.A, R.B, S.B, S.C FROM R RIGHT JOIN S ON R.B = S.B;

    UNION removes the inner rows that appear in both halves. But UNION also removes genuine duplicate rows (if R has two identical rows, the full join should contain both). The bag-correct version keeps all left-join rows and adds only the unmatched right rows:

    SELECT R.A, R.B, S.B, S.C FROM R LEFT JOIN S ON R.B = S.B
UNION ALL
SELECT R.A, R.B, S.B, S.C FROM R RIGHT JOIN S ON R.B = S.B
WHERE  R.A IS NULL;          -- R.A: a column that is never NULL in R (ideally R's key)

    Both give the 8 rows above (checked in SQLite). A RIGHT JOIN can itself be written as a LEFT JOIN with the operands swapped.

    9  Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING · §7.1.7–7.1.8

    Theory recap

    COUNT, SUM, MAX, MIN, AVG summarise a multiset of values into one value; they may appear in SELECT and HAVING (and ORDER BY), never in WHERE. MAX/MIN also work on any totally ordered domain (strings, dates).

    How aggregates treat NULLs
    • NULLs are discarded before SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN and COUNT(col).
    • COUNT(*) counts rows, including rows full of NULLs.
    • On an empty collection (or all NULL): COUNT returns 0; SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN return NULL.
    • COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL values.
    • AVG = SUM / COUNT(col), not SUM / COUNT(*).

    Project 20 has hours 10.0, 15.0, NULL: COUNT(*) = 3, COUNT(Hours) = 2, SUM = 25, AVG = 12.5 (not 8.33). On EMPLOYEE: COUNT(*) = 8, COUNT(Super_ssn) = 7, COUNT(DISTINCT Salary) = 6.

    SELECT SUM(Salary), MAX(Salary), MIN(Salary), AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE;  -- Q19: 281000 55000 25000 35125
SELECT SUM(Salary), MAX(Salary), MIN(Salary), AVG(Salary)                 -- Q20: 133000 40000 25000 33250
FROM   (EMPLOYEE JOIN DEPARTMENT ON Dno = Dnumber) WHERE Dname = 'Research';
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE;                                            -- Q21: 8
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE;                              -- Q23: 6

    GROUP BY

    GROUP BY partitions the rows (after WHERE) into groups with equal values of the grouping attributes; each group yields one output row. NULL grouping values form one group.

    SELECT Dno, COUNT(*), AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno;             -- Q24
SELECT Pnumber, Pname, COUNT(*)                                           -- Q25 (join, then group)
FROM   PROJECT, WORKS_ON WHERE Pnumber = Pno GROUP BY Pnumber, Pname;
SELECT Pnumber, Pname, COUNT(*)                                           -- Q26
FROM   PROJECT, WORKS_ON WHERE Pnumber = Pno
GROUP BY Pnumber, Pname HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
SELECT Pnumber, Pname, COUNT(*)                                           -- Q27
FROM   PROJECT, WORKS_ON, EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Pnumber = Pno AND Ssn = Essn AND Dno = 5 GROUP BY Pnumber, Pname;
