    In Q27, project 30 disappears entirely: no department-5 employee works on it, so it has no rows left after WHERE and hence no group (an inner join never produces a group with count 0; use a LEFT JOIN with the condition in ON to get zeros).

    WHERE vs HAVING (worked past-paper pattern)

    “For each department with more than two employees, count its employees earning more than 30000.”

    Candidate 1 (wrong):

    SELECT Dno, COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary > 30000
GROUP BY Dno
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

    WHERE runs first, so the groups contain only high earners and HAVING tests “more than two employees earning over 30000”. Dept 5 keeps Wong, Narayan (2 rows), dept 4 keeps Wallace (1), dept 1 keeps Borg (1): no group has more than 2 rows. Result: empty.

    Candidate 2 (right, the book’s Q28 pattern): decide which departments are big on the unfiltered table.

    SELECT Dno, COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary > 30000
  AND  Dno IN (SELECT Dno FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno HAVING COUNT(*) > 2)
GROUP BY Dno;

    Big departments: 5 (4 employees) and 4 (3). Result: (5, 2), (4, 1). Equivalent single-pass version: SELECT Dno, SUM(CASE WHEN Salary > 30000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno HAVING COUNT(*) > 2 (this one also reports a big department with zero high earners as 0, which candidate 2 would omit; state which you want).

    Rules for HAVING

    A condition on individual rows belongs in WHERE (it is cheaper and is applied before grouping). A condition on an aggregate must be in HAVING. A HAVING condition may only use grouping columns and aggregates. Moving a row condition from WHERE into HAVING changes nothing only if it is on a grouping column.

    10  WITH, CASE and recursive queries · §7.1.9–7.1.10

    Theory recap

    WITH defines a temporary named table for one query (like a view that is dropped afterwards):

    Q28 rewritten with WITH
    WITH BIGDEPTS (Dno) AS
     ( SELECT Dno FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 )
SELECT Dno, COUNT(*)
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary > 40000 AND Dno IN (SELECT Dno FROM BIGDEPTS)
GROUP BY Dno;

    (The book writes Dno IN BIGDEPTS; standard SQL needs the subquery form shown.)

    CASE gives a value chosen by conditions, usable anywhere a value is allowed:

    U6’: department-dependent raise
    UPDATE EMPLOYEE
SET    Salary = CASE WHEN Dno = 5 THEN Salary + 2000
                     WHEN Dno = 4 THEN Salary + 1500
                     WHEN Dno = 1 THEN Salary + 3000
                     ELSE Salary + 0
                END;

    Recursive queries (SQL:99) compute a fixed point: a base query UNION a recursive part that joins the table being defined with base tables, repeated until no new rows appear.

    Q29: all (supervisor / supervisee) pairs at all levels
    WITH RECURSIVE SUP_EMP (SupSsn, EmpSsn) AS
   ( SELECT Super_ssn, Ssn                  -- base: direct supervision
     FROM   EMPLOYEE
     WHERE  Super_ssn IS NOT NULL
     UNION
     SELECT S.SupSsn, E.Ssn                 -- one more level down
     FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E, SUP_EMP AS S
     WHERE  E.Super_ssn = S.EmpSsn )
SELECT * FROM SUP_EMP;

    On Figure 5.6: 7 direct pairs + 5 second-level pairs (Borg over Smith, Narayan, English, Zelaya, Jabbar) = 12 rows; WHERE SupSsn = ’888665555’ gives all 7 other employees.

    Typos in the printed Q29

    The book uses a column “SupervisorSsn” (the schema calls it Super_ssn) and selects E.Ssn, S.SupSsn in the recursive part, which puts the columns in the wrong order. The version above is corrected and verified.

    11  Query patterns that past papers ask

    Theory recap

    The nnn-th highest value

    -- 2nd highest salary                                             -> 43000
SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE);
-- N-th highest DISTINCT salary: exactly N-1 distinct salaries are larger
SELECT DISTINCT E1.Salary FROM EMPLOYEE E1
WHERE  3 - 1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT E2.Salary)
                FROM   EMPLOYEE E2 WHERE E2.Salary > E1.Salary);  -- N = 3 -> 40000

    Distinct salaries in order: 55000, 43000, 40000, 38000, 30000, 25000. N=6N=6N=6 gives 25000; N=7N=7N=7 gives no row (state what “nnn-th” means when values tie: distinct values, as here, or positions, which would need COUNT(*) and a tie rule). Dialect alternatives: ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 (on SELECT DISTINCT Salary), DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) = N.

    Top-kkk with ties

    “The two lowest-paid employees”: ORDER BY Salary LIMIT 2 returns two of the three employees paid 25000, chosen arbitrarily, which is wrong when ties exist. Keep every employee with fewer than kkk employees strictly below:

    SELECT E1.Fname, E1.Lname, E1.Salary
FROM   EMPLOYEE E1
WHERE  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE E2 WHERE E2.Salary < E1.Salary) < 2;
-- Zelaya, English, Jabbar (all 25000).  Top-3 paid (use >):  Borg, Wallace, Wong

    Window-function version: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary) <= k (RANK gives tied rows the same rank).

    “The X with the largest total”: which candidate queries are correct?

    Project(s) with the largest total hours. Totals: 1: 52.5, 2: 37.5, 3: 50, 10: 55, 20: 25 (the NULL is ignored), 30: 55. Projects 10 and 30 tie.

    CandidateVerdict
    (a)WITH T AS (SELECT Pno, SUM(Hours) AS Total FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno) SELECT Pno, Total FROM T WHERE Total = (SELECT MAX(Total) FROM T);Correct: 10 and 30.
    (b)SELECT Pno FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno HAVING SUM(Hours) >= ALL (SELECT SUM(Hours) FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno);Correct (careful: if some group’s SUM were NULL, ≥\ge≥ ALL would be UNKNOWN for everyone).
    (c)SELECT Pno, SUM(Hours) FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno ORDER BY SUM(Hours) DESC LIMIT 1;Wrong with ties: returns only one of 10, 30 (SQLite gave 30).
    (d)SELECT Pno, MAX(SUM(Hours)) FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno;Invalid in standard SQL (nested aggregate; Oracle allows SELECT MAX(SUM(Hours)) … GROUP BY Pno but then Pno cannot be selected).
    (e)SELECT Pno FROM WORKS_ON WHERE SUM(Hours) = MAX(…) GROUP BY Pno;Invalid: aggregate in WHERE.
    (f)SELECT Pno, MAX(Hours) FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno;Wrong question: the largest single row per project, not the largest total.
    (g)SELECT Pno FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno HAVING SUM(Hours) > 50;Wrong: hard-codes a value read from the data (also returns project 1).

    CUBE-style subtotals without CUBE

    GROUP BY CUBE(Dno, Sex) produces totals for every subset of the grouping columns: (Dno, Sex), (Dno), (Sex), (). Without CUBE, take the UNION ALL of one GROUP BY per subset and put NULL in the rolled-up columns (the columns must line up and be type-compatible):

    SELECT Dno, Sex, SUM(Salary) AS Total FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno, Sex
UNION ALL
SELECT Dno, NULL, SUM(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno
UNION ALL
SELECT NULL, Sex, SUM(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Sex
UNION ALL
SELECT NULL, NULL, SUM(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE;
    DnoSexTotalDnoSexTotalDnoSexTotal
    1M550001NULL55000NULLF93000
    4F680004NULL93000NULLM188000
    4M250005NULL133000NULLNULL281000
    5F25000
    5M108000

    ROLLUP(Dno, Sex) would be only the hierarchical prefixes: (Dno, Sex), (Dno), (). Use UNION ALL: plain UNION could merge a genuine row with an identical subtotal row. If Dno itself could be NULL, a real NULL group and a subtotal row look alike; CUBE solves this with GROUPING(), here add a label column such as ’ALL’ AS Level.

    12  Views · §7.3

    Theory recap

    A view is a single virtual table derived from base tables or other views (its defining tables). It need not be stored, is always up to date and can be queried like any table, but updating it is limited.

    CREATE VIEW WORKS_ON1 AS                                  -- V1: names inherited
SELECT Fname, Lname, Pname, Hours
FROM   EMPLOYEE, PROJECT, WORKS_ON
WHERE  Ssn = Essn AND Pno = Pnumber;
CREATE VIEW DEPT_INFO (Dept_name, No_of_emps, Total_sal) AS   -- V2: names given
SELECT Dname, COUNT(*), SUM(Salary)
FROM   DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Dnumber = Dno
GROUP BY Dname;
SELECT Fname, Lname FROM WORKS_ON1 WHERE Pname = 'ProductX';  -- QV1: Smith, English
DROP VIEW WORKS_ON1;                                          -- V1A

    DEPT_INFO on Figure 5.6: (Administration, 3, 93000), (Headquarters, 1, 55000), (Research, 4, 133000).

    Implementing views

    • Query modification: the DBMS rewrites a query on the view into a query on the base tables (QV1 becomes the three-table join with AND Pname = ’ProductX’ added). Simple, always current; but slow if the view is complex and queried often.
    • View materialization: store the view as a (temporary) table when first queried, and keep it up to date by incremental update (work out which rows to insert/delete/modify after a base-table change). Update policies: immediate (as soon as base tables change), lazy (when the view is next queried), periodic (may return stale data). An unused materialized view may be discarded and recomputed later.
    • An in-line view is a subquery in FROM.

    Updating through a view

    An update on a view must be translated into updates on base tables. It is allowed only when this translation is unambiguous:

    • A view on a single table without aggregates is updatable if it contains the table’s primary key and every NOT NULL column without a default (otherwise an INSERT could not build a full base row).
    • Views on joins are generally not updatable: UV1 (UPDATE WORKS_ON1 SET Pname = ’ProductY’ WHERE Lname = ’Smith’ AND Fname = ’John’ AND Pname = ’ProductX’) could mean (a) move Smith’s WORKS_ON row to project 2 (intended), or (b) rename project ProductX to ProductY (side effect on every row of ProductX).
    • Views with grouping/aggregates are not updatable: UV2 (UPDATE DEPT_INFO SET Total_sal = 100000 WHERE Dept_name = ’Research’) has no meaning on the base rows.
    • WITH CHECK OPTION at the end of the view definition makes the DBMS reject an INSERT/UPDATE through the view that would produce a row not satisfying the view’s WHERE (a row that would vanish from the view).
    Worked example: update and delete through a view (past-paper pattern)
    CREATE VIEW HIGH_PAID AS
SELECT Ssn, Fname, Lname, Salary, Dno
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary > 40000
WITH CHECK OPTION;

    Contents: Wallace (43000, dept 4), Borg (55000, dept 1). Updatable: one table, no aggregate, contains the key Ssn and the NOT NULL columns Fname, Lname, Ssn (Dno is NOT NULL but has DEFAULT 1, and is included anyway).

    1. UPDATE HIGH_PAID SET Salary = Salary * 1.05 WHERE Dno = 4; is translated by query modification into
      UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Salary = Salary * 1.05 WHERE Dno = 4 AND Salary > 40000;
      Only Wallace changes (45150). Zelaya and Jabbar (also dept 4) are untouched: they are not in the view.
    2. UPDATE HIGH_PAID SET Salary = 35000 WHERE Lname = ’Wallace’; is rejected by WITH CHECK OPTION (the row would leave the view). Without the option it succeeds and Wallace silently disappears from HIGH_PAID.
    3. DELETE FROM HIGH_PAID WHERE Dno = 1; becomes DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = 1 AND Salary > 40000;, deleting the base row of Borg. Under the COMPANY constraints this is rejected: Borg is referenced by a WORKS_ON row (RESTRICT) and by DEPARTMENT 1’s Mgr_ssn (SET DEFAULT to ’888665555’, which is Borg himself), so mention the referential constraints when asked “what happens” (Wong’s and Wallace’s Super_ssn alone would just become NULL).
    4. INSERT INTO HIGH_PAID VALUES (’111222333’,’Ann’,’Lee’,30000,5); is rejected by the CHECK OPTION (30000 ≯\not>> 40000).

    Views as an authorization mechanism

    Grant users the privilege on a view but not on the base table: CREATE VIEW DEPT5EMP AS SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = 5; hides other departments’ rows; CREATE VIEW BASIC_EMP_DATA AS SELECT Fname, Lname, Address FROM EMPLOYEE; hides columns such as Salary. (GRANT/REVOKE are in Ch. 30.)

    13  Schema change statements · §7.4

    Theory recap
    DROP SCHEMA COMPANY CASCADE;          -- schema and everything in it
DROP SCHEMA COMPANY RESTRICT;         -- only if the schema is empty
DROP TABLE DEPENDENT CASCADE;         -- also drops FKs/views that reference it
DROP TABLE DEPENDENT RESTRICT;        -- only if nothing references it
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN Job VARCHAR(12);          -- new column = NULL in every row
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE DROP COLUMN Address CASCADE;         -- CASCADE or RESTRICT required
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.DEPARTMENT ALTER COLUMN Mgr_ssn DROP DEFAULT;
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.DEPARTMENT ALTER COLUMN Mgr_ssn SET DEFAULT '333445555';
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE DROP CONSTRAINT EMPSUPERFK CASCADE;  -- needs a named constraint
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE ADD CONSTRAINT EMPSUPERFK
      FOREIGN KEY (Super_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn) ON DELETE SET NULL;
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE ADD CONSTRAINT SAL_POS CHECK (Salary > 0);
    • DROP TABLE removes rows and definition; DELETE FROM T removes only rows.
    • A column added without a default is NULL in all existing rows, so it cannot be NOT NULL unless a DEFAULT is given.
    • Only named constraints can be dropped by name (another reason to name them).
    • Changing a column’s type is dialect-specific (ALTER COLUMN c TYPE … in PostgreSQL, MODIFY c … in MySQL/Oracle).

    14  Database programming · §10.1–10.2

    Theory recap

    Approaches

    ApproachHowExamples
    1. Embedding SQL in a host languageSQL statements marked with a prefix (EXEC SQL); a precompiler extracts them and replaces them by calls to DBMS-generated codeembedded SQL in C; SQLJ in Java (#sql)
    2. Library of functions / classes (API)the program calls functions (connect, prepare, execute, fetch) passing the SQL text as a string parameterSQL/CLI (ODBC), JDBC
    3. New database programming languagea language designed for the data model, adding loops and conditions to SQLOracle PL/SQL, SQL/PSM (stored procedures)

    Approaches 1 and 2 are more common (applications already exist in general-purpose languages); approach 3 suits database-intensive applications and has no impedance mismatch.

    Definition: Impedance mismatch

    The problems caused by the differences between the database model and the programming-language model: (1) type mismatch: SQL types differ from host-language types, so a binding per language is needed (INTEGER →\to→ long, SMALLINT →\to→ short, REAL →\to→ float, DOUBLE →\to→ double, CHAR(iii)/VARCHAR(iii) →\to→ char[i+1i+1i+1] because C strings end with \ 0); (2) set vs. record: a query returns a set/multiset of tuples, while the program handles one record at a time, so a cursor (iterator) is needed to loop over the result and copy each value into program variables.

    Typical sequence of interaction: (1) open a connection to the database server (URL, account, password): CONNECT TO <server> AS <conn> AUTHORIZATION <user/password>; (switch with SET CONNECTION <conn>); (2) submit queries/updates; (3) DISCONNECT <conn>;. Several connections may exist, one active at a time.

    Embedded SQL in C

    • Statements start with EXEC SQL and end with ; (or END-EXEC).
    • Shared (host) variables are declared between EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE SECTION; and EXEC SQL END DECLARE SECTION; and are written with a colon (:ssn) inside SQL, which also lets them share names with columns.
    • Communication variables: SQLCODE (integer: 0 = success, >0>0>0 (100) = no more data, <0<0<0 = error; vendor-specific; in Oracle a field of SQLCA, via EXEC SQL include SQLCA;) and SQLSTATE (5-character string, standardised: ’00000’ = OK, ’02000’ = no more data). Prefer SQLSTATE for portability.
    • A query returning one row can use SELECT … INTO :v1, :v2 …; if it returns several rows, an error is raised, so use a cursor.
    E1: single-row retrieval
    loop = 1;
while (loop) {
  prompt("Enter a Social Security Number: ", ssn);
  EXEC SQL
    SELECT Fname, Minit, Lname, Address, Salary
    INTO   :fname, :minit, :lname, :address, :salary
    FROM   EMPLOYEE WHERE Ssn = :ssn;
  if (SQLCODE == 0) printf(fname, minit, lname, address, salary);
  else printf("Social Security Number does not exist: ", ssn);
  prompt("More Social Security Numbers (enter 1 for Yes, 0 for No): ", loop);
}

    Cursors

    A cursor is a variable that points to one row of a multi-row query result. DECLARE c CURSOR FOR <query> associates it with a query (not yet run); OPEN c executes the query and positions the cursor before the first row; each FETCH c INTO :v… moves to the next row and copies its values; when it moves past the last row SQLCODE >0>0>0 (SQLSTATE ’02000’); CLOSE c releases the result.

    E2: give each employee of a department a raise
    prompt("Enter the Department Name: ", dname);
EXEC SQL SELECT Dnumber INTO :dnumber FROM DEPARTMENT WHERE Dname = :dname;
EXEC SQL DECLARE EMP CURSOR FOR
  SELECT Ssn, Fname, Minit, Lname, Salary
  FROM   EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = :dnumber
  FOR UPDATE OF Salary;
EXEC SQL OPEN EMP;
EXEC SQL FETCH FROM EMP INTO :ssn, :fname, :minit, :lname, :salary;
while (SQLCODE == 0) {
  printf("Employee name is:", fname, minit, lname);
  prompt("Enter the raise amount: ", raise);
  EXEC SQL UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Salary = Salary + :raise
           WHERE CURRENT OF EMP;            -- the row under the cursor
  EXEC SQL FETCH FROM EMP INTO :ssn, :fname, :minit, :lname, :salary;
}
EXEC SQL CLOSE EMP;
    • FOR UPDATE OF <attributes> is required if rows will be updated through the cursor; FOR UPDATE (no list) if rows will be deleted; default is FOR READ ONLY. WHERE CURRENT OF <cursor> targets the current row.

    • General form:

      DECLARE <cursor name> [ INSENSITIVE ] [ SCROLL ] CURSOR
[ WITH HOLD ] FOR <query specification>
[ ORDER BY <ordering specification> ]
[ FOR READ ONLY | FOR UPDATE [ OF <attribute list> ] ] ;
    • SCROLL allows FETCH [NEXT | PRIOR | FIRST | LAST | ABSOLUTE i | RELATIVE i] FROM <cursor> INTO …; the default orientation is NEXT. INSENSITIVE and WITH HOLD concern transactions (Ch. 20).

    Dynamic SQL

    The SQL text is built or read at run time, so it cannot be checked at compile time.

    E3: execute an update typed by the user
    EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE SECTION;
varchar sqlupdatestring[256];
EXEC SQL END DECLARE SECTION;
prompt("Enter the Update Command: ", sqlupdatestring);
EXEC SQL PREPARE sqlcommand FROM :sqlupdatestring;   -- parse/check, generate code once
EXEC SQL EXECUTE sqlcommand;                         -- may be executed many times
-- one-shot alternative:  EXEC SQL EXECUTE IMMEDIATE :sqlupdatestring;

    PREPARE and EXECUTE are separate so a statement executed repeatedly is prepared once, and errors can be caught after PREPARE. Dynamic updates are easy; dynamic queries are harder because the number and types of result columns are unknown when the program is written (needs descriptor structures, as in the API approach).

    SQLJ (SQL embedded in Java)

    • Statements are prefixed with #sql { … }; an SQLJ translator turns them into Java calls through JDBC (so a JDBC driver is needed). Host variables still use :var.

    • Connect (Figure 10.5; true = auto-commit):

      DefaultContext cntxt =
   oracle.getConnection("<url>", "<user>", "<password>", true);
DefaultContext.setDefaultContext(cntxt);
    • Errors are reported as the Java exception SQLException (try {…} catch (SQLException se) {…}), playing the role of SQLCODE/SQLSTATE.
    • Single row: #sql { SELECT … INTO :fname, … FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Ssn = :ssn };

    • Multiple rows use an iterator (like a cursor):

      • named iterator: declares attribute names and types; no INTO needed; next() fetches the next row and controls the loop:

        #sql iterator Emp(String ssn, String fname, String minit, String lname, double salary);
Emp e = null;
#sql e = { SELECT ssn, fname, minit, lname, salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = :dnumber };
while (e.next()) { System.out.println(e.ssn + " " + e.fname + ...); }
e.close();

      • positional iterator: declares only types; rows are read with FETCH, and the loop is controlled by endFetch():

        #sql iterator Emppos(String, String, String, String, double);
#sql e = { SELECT ssn, fname, minit, lname, salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = :dnumber };
#sql { FETCH :e INTO :ssn, :fn, :mi, :ln, :sal };
while (!e.endFetch()) { ...; #sql { FETCH :e INTO :ssn, :fn, :mi, :ln, :sal }; }
e.close();
    Short answers that score on Ch. 10

    “Impedance mismatch” = type mismatch + set-at-a-time vs record-at-a-time; solved by bindings and cursors/iterators. “Why a cursor?” = a SELECT returning several rows cannot be read INTO scalar variables. “Static vs dynamic SQL” = compile-time vs run-time text; PREPARE/EXECUTE. Always mention checking SQLCODE/SQLSTATE after each statement.

    15  Chapter 6 exercises

    Textbook exercises

    How to read this section

    The COMPANY instance (Figure 5.6) and the UNIVERSITY instance (Figure 1.2) are reproduced in Part I, §2. Each query answer gives the SQL, the reasoning, and the result table obtained by running it. Assumptions are written the way the course rewards: stated, then justified.

    6.5Referential integrity and DDL for the UNIVERSITY databaseE&N Ex. 6.5 · p. 203

    Consider the database shown in Figure 1.2, whose schema is shown in Figure 2.1. What are the referential integrity constraints that should hold on the schema? Write appropriate SQL DDL statements to define the database.

    Figure 2.1: STUDENT(Name, Student_number, Class, Major); COURSE(Course_name, Course_number, Credit_hours, Department); PREREQUISITE(Course_number, Prerequisite_number); SECTION(Section_identifier, Course_number, Semester, Year, Instructor); GRADE_REPORT(Student_number, Section_identifier, Grade). (Instance: Part I, §2.2.)

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Keys: STUDENT(Student_number), COURSE(Course_number), SECTION(Section_identifier), PREREQUISITE(Course_number, Prerequisite_number), GRADE_REPORT(Student_number, Section_identifier). Why: these are the identifiers used in Figure 1.2; a course can have several prerequisites and a student several sections, so the two link tables need composite keys.
    2. Major and Department are plain values (there is no DEPARTMENT table in the schema), so they are not foreign keys. Effect: no RI constraint on them.
    3. Class is 1–5 (freshman … graduate, §1.2) and Year is stored as in Figure 1.2 (‘07’, ‘08’), hence CHAR(2).

    Referential integrity constraints

    Foreign keyReferencesMeaning
    SECTION.Course_numberCOURSE.Course_numbera section is an offering of an existing course
    GRADE_REPORT.Student_numberSTUDENT.Student_numbergrades belong to existing students
    GRADE_REPORT.Section_identifierSECTION.Section_identifiergrades are for existing sections
    PREREQUISITE.Course_numberCOURSE.Course_numberthe course that has the prerequisite
    PREREQUISITE.Prerequisite_numberCOURSE.Course_numberthe prerequisite is itself a course

    DDL (executed in SQLite, then loaded with Figure 1.2)

    UNIVERSITY DDL
    CREATE TABLE STUDENT
( Name            VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
  Student_number  INT          NOT NULL,
  Class           INT          CHECK (Class BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  Major           CHAR(4),
  PRIMARY KEY (Student_number) );

CREATE TABLE COURSE
( Course_name     VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  Course_number   CHAR(8)      NOT NULL,
  Credit_hours    INT          CHECK (Credit_hours > 0),
  Department      CHAR(4),
  PRIMARY KEY (Course_number) );

CREATE TABLE PREREQUISITE
( Course_number        CHAR(8)  NOT NULL,
  Prerequisite_number  CHAR(8)  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Course_number, Prerequisite_number),
  FOREIGN KEY (Course_number) REFERENCES COURSE(Course_number)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Prerequisite_number) REFERENCES COURSE(Course_number)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE SECTION
( Section_identifier  INT         NOT NULL,
  Course_number       CHAR(8)     NOT NULL,
  Semester            VARCHAR(6)  NOT NULL,
  Year                CHAR(2)     NOT NULL,
  Instructor          VARCHAR(30),
  PRIMARY KEY (Section_identifier),
  FOREIGN KEY (Course_number) REFERENCES COURSE(Course_number)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE GRADE_REPORT
( Student_number      INT      NOT NULL,
  Section_identifier  INT      NOT NULL,
  Grade               CHAR(1),
  PRIMARY KEY (Student_number, Section_identifier),
  FOREIGN KEY (Student_number) REFERENCES STUDENT(Student_number)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Section_identifier) REFERENCES SECTION(Section_identifier)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );

    Why these triggered actions

    • PREREQUISITE: pure relationship table, so CASCADE on both FKs (if a course disappears, the prerequisite facts about it are meaningless).
    • SECTION.Course_number: RESTRICT on delete (do not lose the history of sections and grades by deleting a course), CASCADE on update (a renumbered course keeps its sections).
    • GRADE_REPORT.Student_number: CASCADE (a grade is a dependent fact of the student; this choice is used in 6.13(d)). GRADE_REPORT.Section_identifier: RESTRICT on delete (deleting a section that has grades would destroy transcripts).
    • ON UPDATE CASCADE everywhere: correcting a key value should follow into every reference.
    Answer

    Five RI constraints: SECTION.Course_number, PREREQUISITE.Course_number and PREREQUISITE.Prerequisite_number all reference COURSE; GRADE_REPORT.Student_number references STUDENT; GRADE_REPORT.Section_identifier references SECTION. DDL as above.

    What the grader checks

    Every FK named with the table it references (both PREREQUISITE columns point to COURSE); composite PKs for the link tables; NOT NULL on key columns; each referential action given a reason. A common loss is declaring Major or Department as an FK to a table that does not exist, or forgetting that Prerequisite_number is also an FK.

    6.6DDL for the AIRLINE schemaE&N Ex. 6.6 · p. 203

    Repeat Exercise 6.5, but use the AIRLINE database schema of Figure 5.8.

    Figure 5.8 (keys underlined): AIRPORT(Airport_code, Name, City, State); FLIGHT(Flight_number, Airline, Weekdays); FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time); LEG_INSTANCE(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Number_of_available_seats, Airplane_id, Departure_airport_code, Departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Arrival_time); FARE(Flight_number, Fare_code, Amount, Restrictions); AIRPLANE_TYPE(Airplane_type_name, Max_seats, Company); CAN_LAND(Airplane_type_name, Airport_code); AIRPLANE(Airplane_id, Total_number_of_seats, Airplane_type); SEAT_RESERVATION(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number, Customer_name, Customer_phone).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Primary keys are the underlined attributes of Figure 5.8. Why: given by the figure.
    2. Departure/arrival airport codes of FLIGHT_LEG and LEG_INSTANCE are NOT NULL in FLIGHT_LEG (a scheduled leg always has both airports) but nullable in LEG_INSTANCE (actual airports may be filled in later).
    3. Date is the attribute name used by the book; in most DBMSs it is a reserved word and must be quoted ("Date") or renamed (Leg_date). Kept here for fidelity.

    Referential integrity constraints (12)

    Referencing attribute(s)ReferencesAction (delete / update)
    FLIGHT_LEG.Flight_numberFLIGHTCASCADE / CASCADE
    FLIGHT_LEG.Departure_airport_codeAIRPORTRESTRICT / CASCADE
    FLIGHT_LEG.Arrival_airport_codeAIRPORTRESTRICT / CASCADE
    LEG_INSTANCE.(Flight_number, Leg_number)FLIGHT_LEGCASCADE / CASCADE
    LEG_INSTANCE.Airplane_idAIRPLANESET NULL / CASCADE
    LEG_INSTANCE.Departure_airport_codeAIRPORTRESTRICT / CASCADE
    LEG_INSTANCE.Arrival_airport_codeAIRPORTRESTRICT / CASCADE
    FARE.Flight_numberFLIGHTCASCADE / CASCADE
    CAN_LAND.Airplane_type_nameAIRPLANE_TYPECASCADE / CASCADE
    CAN_LAND.Airport_codeAIRPORTCASCADE / CASCADE
    AIRPLANE.Airplane_typeAIRPLANE_TYPERESTRICT / CASCADE
    SEAT_RESERVATION.(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date)LEG_INSTANCERESTRICT / CASCADE

    Justification: legs, leg instances and fares are weak/dependent on their flight, so they cascade; CAN_LAND is a relationship table, so it cascades; an airport or airplane type still in use must not vanish (RESTRICT); if an airplane is retired the leg instance survives with the airplane unknown (SET NULL, Airplane_id is not part of the key); a leg instance that has seat reservations must not be deleted silently (RESTRICT protects customers). The FKs are composite: a leg instance references a leg, the pair (Flight_number, Leg_number), and a reservation references the triple.

    DDL (executed in SQLite)

    AIRLINE DDL
    CREATE TABLE AIRPORT
( Airport_code  CHAR(3)      NOT NULL,
  Name          VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  City          VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
  State         VARCHAR(20),
  PRIMARY KEY (Airport_code) );

CREATE TABLE FLIGHT
( Flight_number  VARCHAR(8)   NOT NULL,
  Airline        VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
  Weekdays       VARCHAR(7),
  PRIMARY KEY (Flight_number) );

CREATE TABLE FLIGHT_LEG
( Flight_number             VARCHAR(8)  NOT NULL,
  Leg_number                INT         NOT NULL CHECK (Leg_number >= 1),
  Departure_airport_code    CHAR(3)     NOT NULL,
  Scheduled_departure_time  TIME,
  Arrival_airport_code      CHAR(3)     NOT NULL,
  Scheduled_arrival_time    TIME,
  PRIMARY KEY (Flight_number, Leg_number),
  FOREIGN KEY (Flight_number) REFERENCES FLIGHT(Flight_number)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Departure_airport_code) REFERENCES AIRPORT(Airport_code)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Arrival_airport_code) REFERENCES AIRPORT(Airport_code)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );
    AIRLINE DDL (continued)
    CREATE TABLE AIRPLANE_TYPE
( Airplane_type_name  VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
  Max_seats           INT          NOT NULL CHECK (Max_seats > 0),
  Company             VARCHAR(30),
  PRIMARY KEY (Airplane_type_name) );

CREATE TABLE AIRPLANE
( Airplane_id            VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL,
  Total_number_of_seats  INT          NOT NULL CHECK (Total_number_of_seats > 0),
  Airplane_type          VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Airplane_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (Airplane_type) REFERENCES AIRPLANE_TYPE(Airplane_type_name)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE LEG_INSTANCE
( Flight_number              VARCHAR(8)  NOT NULL,
  Leg_number                 INT         NOT NULL,
  Date                       DATE        NOT NULL,
  Number_of_available_seats  INT         CHECK (Number_of_available_seats >= 0),
  Airplane_id                VARCHAR(10),
  Departure_airport_code     CHAR(3),
  Departure_time             TIME,
  Arrival_airport_code       CHAR(3),
  Arrival_time               TIME,
  PRIMARY KEY (Flight_number, Leg_number, Date),
  FOREIGN KEY (Flight_number, Leg_number)
              REFERENCES FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Airplane_id) REFERENCES AIRPLANE(Airplane_id)
              ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Departure_airport_code) REFERENCES AIRPORT(Airport_code)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Arrival_airport_code) REFERENCES AIRPORT(Airport_code)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );
    AIRLINE DDL (continued)
    CREATE TABLE FARE
( Flight_number  VARCHAR(8)     NOT NULL,
  Fare_code      VARCHAR(10)    NOT NULL,
  Amount         DECIMAL(10,2)  NOT NULL CHECK (Amount >= 0),
  Restrictions   VARCHAR(100),
  PRIMARY KEY (Flight_number, Fare_code),
  FOREIGN KEY (Flight_number) REFERENCES FLIGHT(Flight_number)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE CAN_LAND
( Airplane_type_name  VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
  Airport_code        CHAR(3)      NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Airplane_type_name, Airport_code),
  FOREIGN KEY (Airplane_type_name) REFERENCES AIRPLANE_TYPE(Airplane_type_name)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (Airport_code) REFERENCES AIRPORT(Airport_code)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE SEAT_RESERVATION
( Flight_number   VARCHAR(8)   NOT NULL,
  Leg_number      INT          NOT NULL,
  Date            DATE         NOT NULL,
  Seat_number     VARCHAR(4)   NOT NULL,
  Customer_name   VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  Customer_phone  VARCHAR(15),
  PRIMARY KEY (Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number),
  FOREIGN KEY (Flight_number, Leg_number, Date)
              REFERENCES LEG_INSTANCE(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );
    What the grader checks

    Composite foreign keys must be declared as one constraint over all the columns (FOREIGN KEY (Flight_number, Leg_number) REFERENCES FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number)), not as two separate single-column FKs: Leg_number alone is not a key of anything. Two FKs from one table to AIRPORT (departure and arrival) are both needed.

    6.7Referential actions for LIBRARYE&N Ex. 6.7 · p. 203★ Must-do

    Consider the LIBRARY relational database schema shown in Figure 6.6. Choose the appropriate action (reject, cascade, set to NULL, set to default) for each referential integrity constraint, both for the deletion of a referenced tuple and for the update of a primary key attribute value in a referenced tuple. Justify your choices.

    Figure 6.6: BOOK(Book_id, Title, Publisher_name); BOOK_AUTHORS(Book_id, Author_name); PUBLISHER(Name, Address, Phone); BOOK_COPIES(Book_id, Branch_id, No_of_copies); BOOK_LOANS(Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no, Date_out, Due_date); LIBRARY_BRANCH(Branch_id, Branch_name, Address); BORROWER(Card_no, Name, Address, Phone). Arrows: BOOK.Publisher_name → PUBLISHER.Name; BOOK_AUTHORS.Book_id, BOOK_COPIES.Book_id, BOOK_LOANS.Book_id → BOOK; BOOK_COPIES.Branch_id, BOOK_LOANS.Branch_id → LIBRARY_BRANCH; BOOK_LOANS.Card_no → BORROWER.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The seven FKs are exactly the arrows of Figure 6.6. Why: the figure draws them.
    2. SET NULL is impossible for an FK that is part of the referencing table’s primary key (entity integrity), which rules it out for all FKs except BOOK.Publisher_name. Effect: only CASCADE, RESTRICT or SET DEFAULT remain for the others.
    3. No sensible default book, branch or borrower exists, so SET DEFAULT is not used.
    4. Library policy: a loan record represents a physical book currently out; it must not disappear as a side effect.
    FK → referencedON DELETEON UPDATEJustification
    BOOK. Publisher_name → PUBLISHERSET NULLCASCADEThe book stays in the catalogue if the publisher record is removed; the publisher just becomes unknown. Publisher_name is not part of BOOK’s key, so NULL is allowed. (RESTRICT is also defensible.)
    BOOK_AUTHORS. Book_id → BOOKCASCADECASCADERepresents the multivalued attribute “authors” of a book; meaningless without the book.
    BOOK_COPIES. Book_id → BOOKCASCADECASCADECopy counts describe the book; if the title is withdrawn from the catalogue, its copy counts go too.
    BOOK_COPIES. Branch_id → LIBRARY_BRANCHCASCADECASCADECopy counts of a closed branch are meaningless.
    BOOK_LOANS. Book_id → BOOKRESTRICTCASCADEA book that is out on loan must not be deleted (we would lose track of who has it).
    BOOK_LOANS. Branch_id → LIBRARY_BRANCHRESTRICTCASCADEA branch with outstanding loans cannot be closed until the books are returned.
    BOOK_LOANS. Card_no → BORROWERRESTRICTCASCADEA borrower who still has books cannot be removed.

    Why ON UPDATE CASCADE everywhere: a key value is changed only to correct it (e.g. a mistyped Book_id or a reissued card number); every reference should follow automatically, and rejecting would force deleting and re-inserting all referencing rows.

    Interaction to note: deleting a BOOK cascades to BOOK_AUTHORS and BOOK_COPIES but is RESTRICTed by BOOK_LOANS; since a statement is atomic, the whole delete is rejected while the book is on loan (checked in SQLite: deleting a book with a loan fails, deleting one without loans removes its copies and authors).

    Answer

    SET NULL/CASCADE for Publisher_name; CASCADE/CASCADE for BOOK_AUTHORS.Book_id, BOOK_COPIES.Book_id and BOOK_COPIES.Branch_id; RESTRICT (reject)/CASCADE for the three FKs of BOOK_LOANS.

    What the grader checks

    Graders want both a delete action and an update action for every FK, each with a reason. Common losses: choosing SET NULL for an FK that is part of a primary key (violates entity integrity); cascading deletes into BOOK_LOANS (silently loses who holds a book) without comment; giving one blanket answer for all FKs. Alternative choices are accepted when justified (e.g. RESTRICT for the publisher).

    6.8DDL for LIBRARYE&N Ex. 6.8 · p. 203

    Write appropriate SQL DDL statements for declaring the LIBRARY relational database schema of Figure 6.6. Specify the keys and referential triggered actions.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Referential actions as chosen and justified in Exercise 6.7. Why: consistency.
    2. Tables are created parents first (PUBLISHER, BOOK, BRANCH, BORROWER, then the dependent tables), so no FK refers to a table that does not exist yet.
    3. No_of_copies ≥\ge≥ 0 and Due_date ≥\ge≥ Date_out are natural CHECKs; Title and names are required.
    LIBRARY DDL (executed in SQLite with foreign keys on)
    CREATE TABLE PUBLISHER
( Name     VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  Address  VARCHAR(60),
  Phone    VARCHAR(15),
  PRIMARY KEY (Name) );

CREATE TABLE BOOK
( Book_id         INT          NOT NULL,
  Title           VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL,
  Publisher_name  VARCHAR(40),
  PRIMARY KEY (Book_id),
  CONSTRAINT BOOK_PUB_FK FOREIGN KEY (Publisher_name) REFERENCES PUBLISHER(Name)
              ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE BOOK_AUTHORS
( Book_id      INT          NOT NULL,
  Author_name  VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Book_id, Author_name),
  CONSTRAINT BA_BOOK_FK FOREIGN KEY (Book_id) REFERENCES BOOK(Book_id)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE LIBRARY_BRANCH
( Branch_id    INT          NOT NULL,
  Branch_name  VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  Address      VARCHAR(60),
  PRIMARY KEY (Branch_id) );

CREATE TABLE BORROWER
( Card_no  INT          NOT NULL,
  Name     VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
  Address  VARCHAR(60),
  Phone    VARCHAR(15),
  PRIMARY KEY (Card_no) );

CREATE TABLE BOOK_COPIES
( Book_id       INT  NOT NULL,
  Branch_id     INT  NOT NULL,
  No_of_copies  INT  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (No_of_copies >= 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (Book_id, Branch_id),
  CONSTRAINT BC_BOOK_FK FOREIGN KEY (Book_id) REFERENCES BOOK(Book_id)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT BC_BRANCH_FK FOREIGN KEY (Branch_id) REFERENCES LIBRARY_BRANCH(Branch_id)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE );

CREATE TABLE BOOK_LOANS
( Book_id    INT   NOT NULL,
  Branch_id  INT   NOT NULL,
  Card_no    INT   NOT NULL,
  Date_out   DATE  NOT NULL,
  Due_date   DATE  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no),
  CONSTRAINT BL_DATES CHECK (Due_date >= Date_out),
  CONSTRAINT BL_BOOK_FK FOREIGN KEY (Book_id) REFERENCES BOOK(Book_id)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT BL_BRANCH_FK FOREIGN KEY (Branch_id) REFERENCES LIBRARY_BRANCH(Branch_id)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT BL_BORROWER_FK FOREIGN KEY (Card_no) REFERENCES BORROWER(Card_no)
              ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE );

    Tested: deleting a book that is on loan is rejected; deleting a book with no loan removes its copies; deleting the publisher sets the remaining book’s Publisher_name to NULL; changing a borrower’s Card_no updates the loan row.

    What the grader checks

    Checks: a PRIMARY KEY in every table (composite for BOOK_AUTHORS, BOOK_COPIES, BOOK_LOANS); all seven FKs; an action for both ON DELETE and ON UPDATE that matches the justification in 6.7; NOT NULL on key columns. Naming the constraints is good practice (they can be dropped later).

    6.9How the DBMS enforces key and foreign key constraintsE&N Ex. 6.9 · p. 203

    How can the key and foreign key constraints be enforced by the DBMS? Is the enforcement technique you suggest difficult to implement? Can the constraint checks be executed efficiently when updates are applied to the database?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Key (PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE) constraints

    The DBMS builds an index (B+^++-tree or hash) on the key attributes. On every INSERT, or UPDATE of a key attribute, it looks the new value up in the index: if found, the operation is rejected; otherwise the row is stored and the index entry added. PRIMARY KEY additionally checks the value is not NULL (entity integrity). DELETE needs no check.

    Foreign key (referential integrity) constraints

    • INSERT into / UPDATE of the FK in the referencing table: look up the FK value in the referenced table’s primary-key index; reject if absent (a NULL FK is allowed unless NOT NULL).
    • DELETE from / UPDATE of the key in the referenced table: find every referencing row with that value and apply the declared action (reject, cascade, set NULL, set default). Doing this fast needs an index on the FK column of each referencing table; without it each delete scans the whole referencing table.
    • Cascades may chain (EMPLOYEE →\to→ WORKS_ON, DEPENDENT, …) and must be applied atomically with the triggering statement (all or nothing); circular references need checks deferred to the end of the transaction.

    Difficulty and efficiency

    Implementation is not hard: it reuses the indexes the DBMS already maintains, and each check is a single index lookup, O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) with a B+^++-tree (about constant with hashing), so checks on single-row inserts and updates are cheap. The cost grows when (a) the FK side has no index (full scans on parent deletes), (b) many rows are affected (bulk loads, cascades touching many rows), or (c) checks must be deferred and verified at commit. Systems therefore index PKs automatically, advise indexing FKs, and allow disabling/deferring constraints during bulk loading.

    Answer

    Enforce keys with a unique index checked on insert/update; enforce FKs by an index lookup in the parent on child insert/update and by locating referencing rows (index on the FK) on parent delete/update, then applying the triggered action. With indexes, every check is one index probe, so it is efficient; it is costly only for unindexed FKs, large cascades and bulk updates.

    6.10COMPANY queries with resultsE&N Ex. 6.10 · p. 203★ Must-do

    Specify the following queries in SQL on the COMPANY relational database schema shown in Figure 5.5. Show the result of each query if it is applied to the COMPANY database in Figure 5.6.

    1. Retrieve the names of all employees in department 5 who work more than 10 hours per week on the ProductX project.
    2. List the names of all employees who have a dependent with the same first name as themselves.
    3. Find the names of all employees who are directly supervised by ‘Franklin Wong’.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Names” means first and last name (Fname, Lname). Why: the schema splits a name into Fname, Minit, Lname and the book’s own queries return Fname, Lname.
    2. Pname is unique (UNIQUE (Pname) in Fig. 6.1), so Pname = ’ProductX’ identifies one project; and Fname + Lname identify Franklin Wong (only one in the instance). If names could repeat, (c) would return the supervisees of every Franklin Wong.
    3. “More than 10 hours” is strict (>>> 10). A NULL Hours value is UNKNOWN in the comparison and is not returned.

    (a) Department 5, more than 10 hours on ProductX

    6.10(a)
    SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E, WORKS_ON AS W, PROJECT AS P
WHERE  E.Dno = 5
  AND  E.Ssn = W.Essn AND W.Pno = P.Pnumber          -- join conditions
  AND  P.Pname = 'ProductX' AND W.Hours > 10;        -- selection conditions

    Working: ProductX is Pnumber 1; WORKS_ON rows for Pno 1 are (123456789, 32.5) and (453453453, 20.0); both are in department 5 and both exceed 10 hours.

    FnameLname
    JohnSmith
    JoyceEnglish

    (b) Dependent with the same first name

    6.10(b)
    SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E, DEPENDENT AS D
WHERE  E.Ssn = D.Essn                     -- the dependent belongs to this employee
  AND  E.Fname = D.Dependent_name;

    Equivalent: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM DEPENDENT D WHERE D.Essn = E.Ssn AND D.Dependent_name = E.Fname) (this form also avoids duplicates if an employee had two such dependents). Working: dependents’ names are Alice, Theodore, Joy (of Wong), Abner (of Wallace), Michael, Alice, Elizabeth (of Smith); none equals the employee’s own first name (Franklin, Jennifer, John). Result: no rows.

    FnameLname
    (no rows)

    (c) Directly supervised by Franklin Wong

    6.10(c): self-join
    SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E, EMPLOYEE AS S             -- S plays the supervisor role
WHERE  E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn
  AND  S.Fname = 'Franklin' AND S.Lname = 'Wong';
    6.10(c): nested alternative
    SELECT Fname, Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Super_ssn IN (SELECT Ssn FROM EMPLOYEE
                     WHERE Fname = 'Franklin' AND Lname = 'Wong');

    Working: Wong’s Ssn is 333445555; employees with Super_ssn = 333445555 are Smith, Narayan, English. “Directly” excludes the indirect level (no one is supervised by Wong’s supervisees).

    FnameLname
    JohnSmith
    RameshNarayan
    JoyceEnglish
    Answer

    (a) John Smith, Joyce English. (b) No rows. (c) John Smith, Ramesh Narayan, Joyce English.

    What the grader checks

    Per query: correct tables in FROM; every join condition present (a missing one gives a Cartesian product); the right selection conditions; the self-join in (c) with two aliases; the result table shown. Writing an empty result explicitly for (b) (with the reason) earns the result mark; leaving it blank does not.

    6.11The updates of “Exercise 3.11” in SQLE&N Ex. 6.11 · p. 204

    Specify the updates of Exercise 3.11 using the SQL update commands.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The cross-reference is wrong in this edition. Exercise 3.11 asks “What is meant by a recursive relationship type?” and contains no updates. The intended exercise is 5.11 (“Suppose that each of the following Update operations is applied directly to the database state shown in Figure 5.6 …”), which is the update-operations exercise on the COMPANY schema (it was numbered 3.11 in earlier editions, where the relational model was Chapter 3).
    2. Each operation is applied independently to the Figure 5.6 state (as 5.11 says), under the Figure 6.1 constraints (no triggered actions, i.e. the default RESTRICT).
    3. Values are written with the types of Figure 6.1 (Hours numeric, so ‘40.0’ becomes 40.0).

    Exercise 5.11’s operations and their SQL; the last column is what a DBMS enforcing Figure 6.1 does (each statement was run in SQLite on a fresh copy of Figure 5.6 with foreign keys on).

    5.11 updates in SQL
    -- a.
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE VALUES ('Robert','F','Scott','943775543','1972-06-21',
       '2365 Newcastle Rd, Bellaire, TX','M',58000,'888665555',1);
-- b.
INSERT INTO PROJECT VALUES ('ProductA', 4, 'Bellaire', 2);
-- c.
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT VALUES ('Production', 4, '943775543', '2007-10-01');
-- d.
INSERT INTO WORKS_ON VALUES ('677678989', NULL, 40.0);
-- e.
INSERT INTO DEPENDENT VALUES ('453453453', 'John', 'M', '1990-12-12', 'spouse');
-- f.
DELETE FROM WORKS_ON WHERE Essn = '333445555';
-- g.
DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Ssn = '987654321';
-- h.
DELETE FROM PROJECT WHERE Pname = 'ProductX';
-- i.
UPDATE DEPARTMENT SET Mgr_ssn = '123456789', Mgr_start_date = '2007-10-01'
WHERE  Dnumber = 5;
-- j.
UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Super_ssn = '943775543' WHERE Ssn = '999887777';
-- k.
UPDATE WORKS_ON SET Hours = 5.0 WHERE Essn = '999887777' AND Pno = 10;
    Effect on Figure 5.6 (constraints of Figure 6.1)
    aAccepted (Ssn new, Super_ssn 888665555 and Dno 1 exist).
    bRejected: referential integrity, Dnum = 2 does not exist (Pnumber 4 and Pname are new, so keys are fine).
    cRejected: key constraint, Dnumber 4 already exists; also RI, Mgr_ssn 943775543 does not exist (unless (a) ran first).
    dRejected: entity integrity, Pno is part of the key and is NULL; also RI, Essn 677678989 does not exist.
    eAccepted (Essn 453453453 exists; key (453453453, John) is new).
    fAccepted: 4 rows deleted (nothing references WORKS_ON).
    gRejected: 987654321 (Wallace) is referenced by Super_ssn of Zelaya and Jabbar, by DEPARTMENT 4’s Mgr_ssn, by WORKS_ON and by DEPENDENT. Alternatives: cascade, set NULL for Super_ssn, or reassign the references first.
    hRejected: Pnumber 1 is referenced by WORKS_ON rows of Smith and English (alternative: cascade into WORKS_ON).
    iAccepted (123456789 exists).
    jRejected: RI, 943775543 is not an existing Ssn (accepted only if (a) is applied first).
    kAccepted (Hours is not a key or FK).
    Answer

    The eleven SQL statements above (INSERT INTO … VALUES for a–e, DELETE FROM … WHERE for f–h, UPDATE … SET … WHERE for i–k), interpreting “Exercise 3.11” as Exercise 5.11. Under RESTRICT, b, c, d, g, h, j are rejected.

    What the grader checks

    State the typo and the exercise you used: a stated, sensible reading of a wrong cross-reference gets full credit. Each DELETE/UPDATE needs a WHERE that selects exactly the intended rows (a key, or the full key for WORKS_ON in (k)).

    6.12UNIVERSITY queriesE&N Ex. 6.12 · p. 204

    Specify the following queries in SQL on the database schema of Figure 1.2.

    1. Retrieve the names of all senior students majoring in ‘cs’ (computer science).
    2. Retrieve the names of all courses taught by Professor King in 2007 and 2008.
    3. For each section taught by Professor King, retrieve the course number, semester, year, and number of students who took the section.
    4. Retrieve the name and transcript of each senior student (Class = 4) majoring in CS. A transcript includes course name, course number, credit hours, semester, year, and grade for each course completed by the student.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Senior” means Class = 4 (stated in part d). Major is stored as ‘CS’ in Figure 1.2; string comparison is case-sensitive, so we compare with ’CS’ (writing ’cs’ as printed would return nothing; a robust version is UPPER(Major) = ’CS’).
    2. Year is stored as two digits (‘07’, ‘08’), so 2007 and 2008 are ’07’ and ’08’.
    3. (b) “in 2007 and 2008” is read as “in 2007 or in 2008” (courses King taught in either year). The stricter reading “in both years” is shown too.
    4. (c) The number of students = number of GRADE_REPORT rows of the section (key (Student_number, Section_identifier), so no student is counted twice). Sections with no students should show 0, so a LEFT JOIN is used.
    5. (d) “Completed” = there is a grade-report row with a non-NULL grade.

    (a)

    6.12(a)
    SELECT Name
FROM   STUDENT
WHERE  Class = 4 AND Major = 'CS';

    Result on Figure 1.2: no rows (Smith is Class 1, Brown is Class 2).

    (b)

    6.12(b): taught by King in 2007 or 2008
    SELECT DISTINCT C.Course_name
FROM   COURSE AS C, SECTION AS S
WHERE  C.Course_number = S.Course_number
  AND  S.Instructor = 'King'
  AND  S.Year IN ('07', '08');

    DISTINCT because King may teach several sections of one course. Result: Discrete Mathematics (section 85, Fall 07). The “both years” reading intersects the two years:

    6.12(b): taught by King in both years
    SELECT C.Course_name FROM COURSE C
WHERE  C.Course_number IN (SELECT Course_number FROM SECTION
                           WHERE  Instructor = 'King' AND Year = '07')
  AND  C.Course_number IN (SELECT Course_number FROM SECTION
                           WHERE  Instructor = 'King' AND Year = '08');

    Result: no rows (King has no 2008 section).

    (c)

    6.12(c)
    SELECT   S.Course_number, S.Semester, S.Year,
         COUNT(G.Student_number) AS Num_students      -- 0 for a section with no grades
FROM     SECTION AS S LEFT OUTER JOIN GRADE_REPORT AS G
         ON S.Section_identifier = G.Section_identifier
WHERE    S.Instructor = 'King'
GROUP BY S.Section_identifier, S.Course_number, S.Semester, S.Year;

    Group by Section_identifier (one row per section; two sections of one course in one term must not merge), plus the other selected columns as standard SQL requires. COUNT(G.Student_number), not COUNT(*), so that an empty section counts 0.

    Course_numberSemesterYearNum_students
    MATH2410Fall071

    (d)

    6.12(d)
    SELECT   ST.Name, C.Course_name, C.Course_number, C.Credit_hours,
         S.Semester, S.Year, G.Grade
FROM     STUDENT AS ST, GRADE_REPORT AS G, SECTION AS S, COURSE AS C
WHERE    ST.Class = 4 AND ST.Major = 'CS'
  AND    ST.Student_number = G.Student_number
  AND    G.Section_identifier = S.Section_identifier
  AND    S.Course_number = C.Course_number
  AND    G.Grade IS NOT NULL                   -- completed courses only
ORDER BY ST.Name, S.Year, S.Semester;

    Result: no rows (no senior). Sanity check with Class = 2 instead returns Brown’s transcript:

    NameCourse_nameCourse_numberCredit_hoursSemesterYearGrade
    BrownDiscrete MathematicsMATH24103Fall07A
    BrownIntro to Computer ScienceCS13104Fall07A
    BrownDatabaseCS33803Fall08A
    BrownData StructuresCS33204Spring08B

    (Spring sorts after Fall alphabetically; a true chronological order would need a semester-order column.)

    Answer

    (a) and (d) return no rows on Figure 1.2; (b) Discrete Mathematics (no rows under the “both years” reading); (c) (MATH2410, Fall, 07, 1).

    What the grader checks

    (c) is the one graded hardest: group by the section (not by course), count students (not rows of a join that duplicates them), and keep empty sections if you claim to. A missing join condition in the four-table join of (d) is the commonest error. Mention the ‘cs’ vs ‘CS’ case issue as an assumption.

    6.13UNIVERSITY updatesE&N Ex. 6.13 · p. 205

    Write SQL update statements to do the following on the database schema shown in Figure 1.2.

    1. Insert a new student, <<<‘Johnson’, 25, 1, ‘Math’>>>, in the database.
    2. Change the class of student ‘Smith’ to 2.

    2. The DDL of Exercise 6.5 is in force (GRADE_REPORT.Student_number ON DELETE CASCADE).
    6.13
    -- a. column order of STUDENT: Name, Student_number, Class, Major
INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES ('Johnson', 25, 1, 'Math');
-- b. (if several students were called Smith, all would change: use the key to be safe)

    6.15CASCADE on the supervisor foreign keyE&N Ex. 6.15 · p. 205

    Consider that the EMPLOYEE table’s constraint EMPSUPERFK as specified in Figure 6.2 is changed to read as follows:

    CONSTRAINT EMPSUPERFK
  FOREIGN KEY (Super_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn)
              ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,

    Answer the following questions:

    1. What happens when the following command is run on the database state shown in Figure 5.6?
      DELETE EMPLOYEE WHERE Lname = ’Borg’
    2. Is it better to CASCADE or SET NULL in case of EMPSUPERFK constraint ON DELETE?
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The command means DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Lname = ’Borg’; (standard SQL needs FROM; the printed form is Oracle-style shorthand).
    2. Two readings of “the rest of the schema”: (i) the question’s intent, looking only at EMPSUPERFK; (ii) the full schema of Figures 6.1/6.2 with every other FK unchanged. Both are answered.

    (a)(i) Effect of the cascade through the supervision hierarchy

    1. Borg (888665555) is deleted.
    2. ON DELETE CASCADE deletes every employee whose Super_ssn = 888665555: Wong and Wallace.
    3. Their deletion cascades again: Super_ssn = 333445555 gives Smith, Narayan, English; Super_ssn = 987654321 gives Zelaya, Jabbar.
    4. Those five supervise nobody, so the cascade stops.

    All 8 employees are deleted: the EMPLOYEE table becomes empty because Borg is the root of the supervision tree. (Verified in SQLite with recursive cascading: 0 rows remain.)

    (a)(ii) With the other constraints of Figures 6.1/6.2

    The deleted employees are still referenced elsewhere: WORKS_ON.Essn and DEPENDENT.Essn have no triggered action (RESTRICT), and DEPARTMENT.Mgr_ssn has ON DELETE SET DEFAULT with default ‘888665555’, which is Borg himself and is being deleted. These violations make the DBMS reject the whole DELETE; since a statement is atomic, nothing is deleted (verified: SQLite reports a foreign key failure and the table is unchanged).

    (b) CASCADE or SET NULL?

    SET NULL is better. Supervision is an optional relationship between two independent employees: when a supervisor leaves, the subordinates still work for the company and should only lose their supervisor value (to be reassigned later). CASCADE treats the subordinates as dependent on the supervisor, so deleting one person can wipe out a whole subtree of the organisation, as (a) shows (the entire company). CASCADE fits weak entities and relationship tables (DEPENDENT, WORKS_ON), not a self-referencing link between peers. (ON UPDATE CASCADE remains correct: a corrected Ssn should propagate.)

    Answer

    (a) The cascade deletes Borg, then Wong and Wallace, then Smith, Narayan, English, Zelaya and Jabbar: all 8 employees. With the other COMPANY FKs in force (WORKS_ON, DEPENDENT RESTRICT; DEPARTMENT.Mgr_ssn SET DEFAULT to Borg) the statement is rejected and nothing changes. (b) SET NULL.

    What the grader checks

    Full marks need the chain: Borg →\to→ Wong, Wallace →\to→ the five others, ending with an empty table; stopping after Wong and Wallace is the typical partial answer. Mentioning the other referencing tables (and that the statement is atomic) also earns credit. Part (b) needs the reason (independent entities, mass deletion), not just “SET NULL”.
