    7.1The six clauses of an SQL queryE&N Ex. 7.1 · p. 236

    Describe the six clauses in the syntax of an SQL retrieval query. Show what type of constructs can be specified in each of the six clauses. Which of the six clauses are required and which are optional?

    Solution · written for this guide

    An SQL retrieval query has up to six clauses, written in this order:

    General form
    SELECT   <attribute and function list>      -- required
FROM     <table list>                       -- required
[ WHERE    <condition> ]                    -- optional
[ GROUP BY <grouping attribute(s)> ]        -- optional
[ HAVING   <group condition> ]              -- optional (needs groups)
[ ORDER BY <attribute list> [ASC|DESC] ] ;  -- optional
    ClauseStatusConstructs allowed in it
    SELECTrequiredThe output columns: attributes (E.Lname), *, DISTINCT / ALL, arithmetic expressions (1.1*Salary), renaming with AS, aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT(DISTINCT x)), CASE expressions, scalar nested queries.
    FROMrequiredThe tables the query reads: base tables, views, tuple variables (aliases, e.g. EMPLOYEE AS E), joined tables (JOIN … ON, NATURAL JOIN, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN, CROSS JOIN), nested queries used as tables (in-line views). Tables used only inside nested queries are not listed here.
    WHEREoptionalA condition on individual tuples: selection and join conditions with =, <>, <, <=, >, >=, AND/OR/NOT, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS [NOT] NULL, IN, EXISTS, UNIQUE, op ANY/SOME/ALL, nested and correlated nested queries. No aggregates directly.
    GROUP BYoptionalThe grouping attributes: tuples with equal values form one group; aggregates in SELECT/HAVING are computed per group.
    HAVINGoptionalA condition on groups: it may use aggregates (COUNT(*) > 2, AVG(Salary) > 30000), grouping attributes and nested queries. Used together with GROUP BY (without it the whole result is one group).
    ORDER BYoptionalThe order of the result rows: attributes or expressions, each ASC (default) or DESC; several keys break ties left to right.
    Answer

    The six clauses are SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Only SELECT and FROM are required; the other four are optional (and HAVING only makes sense with groups).

    7.2Conceptual order of evaluationE&N Ex. 7.2 · p. 236★ Must-do

    Describe conceptually how an SQL retrieval query will be executed by specifying the conceptual order of executing each of the six clauses.

    Solution · written for this guide

    The clauses are written as SELECT–FROM–WHERE–GROUP BY–HAVING–ORDER BY, but they are evaluated conceptually in this order:

    StepClauseWhat it does
    1FROMBuilds the input: the Cartesian product of all listed tables, or the joined tables (JOIN … ON, outer joins) are materialised.
    2WHEREKeeps only the tuple combinations for which the condition is true (false and unknown are both dropped).
    3GROUP BYPartitions the remaining tuples into groups with equal grouping values.
    4HAVINGKeeps only the groups for which the group condition is true.
    5SELECTComputes the output columns (one row per tuple, or one row per group with its aggregates); then DISTINCT, if present, removes duplicate rows.
    6ORDER BYSorts the final result.

    Without GROUP BY/HAVING/ORDER BY the meaning is: for each combination of tuples, one from each table in FROM, evaluate WHERE; if it is true, output the SELECT attributes of that combination. This is only a way to understand the meaning of a query: the DBMS optimiser may run it in any order that gives the same result.

    Worked example on Figure 5.6

    For each department with more than one employee earning over $25,000, list the department name and the number of such employees, largest first.

    Example query
    SELECT   Dname, COUNT(*) AS Num_high          -- step 5
FROM     EMPLOYEE JOIN DEPARTMENT ON Dno = Dnumber   -- step 1
WHERE    Salary > 25000                       -- step 2
GROUP BY Dname                                -- step 3
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 1                         -- step 4
ORDER BY Num_high DESC;                       -- step 6
    1. FROM: the join gives all 8 employees, each with its department.
    2. WHERE: Salary >>> 25000 keeps 5 rows: Smith, Wong, Narayan (Research), Wallace (Administration), Borg (Headquarters).
    3. GROUP BY Dname: groups Research (3 rows), Administration (1), Headquarters (1).
    4. HAVING COUNT(*) >>> 1: only Research survives.
    5. SELECT: (Research, 3).   6. ORDER BY: one row, nothing to sort.

    Verified result: (Research, 3).

    Consequences of the order (exam favourites)
    • WHERE runs before grouping, so it cannot contain aggregates: WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 is illegal; use HAVING.
    • A WHERE condition changes which tuples are counted/averaged; a HAVING condition only chooses groups (see Exercise 7.5b).
    • A column alias defined in SELECT (Num_high) can be used in ORDER BY (which runs after SELECT) but not in WHERE.
    • A non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY, because SELECT runs on whole groups.
    Answer

    Conceptual order: FROM →\rightarrow→ WHERE →\rightarrow→ GROUP BY →\rightarrow→ HAVING →\rightarrow→ SELECT (then DISTINCT) →\rightarrow→ ORDER BY.

    7.3NULLs in comparisons, aggregates and groupingE&N Ex. 7.3 · p. 236★ Must-do

    Discuss how NULLs are treated in comparison operators in SQL. How are NULLs treated when aggregate functions are applied in an SQL query? How are NULLs treated if they exist in grouping attributes?

    Solution · written for this guide

    NULL means a missing value (unknown, withheld or not applicable); SQL does not distinguish the three, and treats every NULL as different from every other NULL.

    1. Comparisons: three-valued logic

    Any comparison (=, <>, <, >, …) in which an operand is NULL gives unknown, not true or false. Even NULL = NULL is unknown. Conditions are combined with Table 7.1:

    ANDtruefalseunknown
    truetruefalseunknown
    falsefalsefalsefalse
    unknownunknownfalseunknown

     

    ORtruefalseunknown
    truetruetruetrue
    falsetruefalseunknown
    unknowntrueunknownunknown

     

    NOT
    truefalse
    falsetrue
    unknownunknown

    A WHERE (or HAVING, or join ON) condition selects a row only if it is true; false and unknown rows are dropped. Examples on Figure 5.6 (Borg has Super_ssn = NULL):

    • WHERE Super_ssn <> ’333445555’ returns Wong, Zelaya, Wallace, Jabbar, but not Borg: for Borg the test is unknown.
    • WHERE Super_ssn = NULL never returns a row. The correct test is IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, which always gives true/false: WHERE Super_ssn IS NULL returns James Borg (Query 18).
    • WHERE NOT (Hours > 12) on project 20 returns only (333445555, 20, 10.0); Borg’s row with Hours NULL gives NOT(unknown) = unknown and is dropped. So “¬C\neg C¬C” rows and “CCC” rows together need not cover the table.
    • Joins: a NULL join attribute matches nothing, so Borg disappears from EMPLOYEE E JOIN EMPLOYEE S ON E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn (7 rows, not 8). Only an outer join keeps him (with NULLs for the supervisor).
    NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery

    x NOT IN (v1, v2, NULL) means x<>v1 AND x<>v2 AND x<>NULL; the last term is unknown, so the whole condition is never true. On Figure 5.6, “employees who supervise nobody”:

    NOT IN trap
    SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Ssn NOT IN (SELECT Super_ssn FROM EMPLOYEE);    -- returns NO rows!

    returns nothing, because Borg’s NULL Super_ssn is in the subquery. Fix it with … WHERE Super_ssn IS NOT NULL inside the subquery, or use NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE S WHERE S.Super_ssn = E.Ssn). Both return the correct 5 employees: Smith, Zelaya, Narayan, English, Jabbar (verified).

    2. Aggregate functions

    • SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT(col) first discard NULLs from the collection, then compute.
    • COUNT(*) counts rows, so rows with NULLs are counted.
    • If the collection is empty (or all NULL): COUNT gives 0, all the others give NULL.
    • COUNT(DISTINCT col) ignores NULLs and duplicates.

    Example: project 20 has Hours 10.0, 15.0, NULL.

    COUNT(*)COUNT(Hours)SUM(Hours)AVG(Hours)
    3225.012.5 (= 25/2, not 25/3)

    Also COUNT(*), COUNT(Super_ssn), COUNT(DISTINCT Super_ssn) over EMPLOYEE give 8, 7, 3; and on an empty selection (WHERE Dno = 7) COUNT(*) = 0 but SUM(Salary) = MAX(Salary) = NULL.

    3. NULLs in grouping attributes (and DISTINCT)

    Although NULL ≠\neq= NULL in comparisons, for GROUP BY all tuples with NULL in the grouping attribute form one separate group.

    SELECT Super_ssn, COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Super_ssn;

    Super_ssnCOUNT(*)
    NULL1
    3334455553
    8886655552
    9876543212

    Similarly SELECT DISTINCT and UNION keep one NULL (NULLs are treated as duplicates of each other there).

    Answer

    Comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN (three-valued logic); WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, so test NULL with IS [NOT] NULL. Aggregates ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)); an empty collection gives COUNT = 0 and NULL for the rest. In GROUP BY all NULL values of the grouping attribute form one separate group.

    7.4Survey of SQL constructsE&N Ex. 7.4 · p. 236

    Discuss how each of the following constructs is used in SQL, and discuss the various options for each construct. Specify what each construct is useful for. (a) Nested queries; (b) Joined tables and outer joins; (c) Aggregate functions and grouping; (d) Triggers; (e) Assertions and how they differ from triggers; (f) The SQL WITH clause; (g) SQL CASE construct; (h) Views and their updatability; (i) Schema change commands.

    Solution · written for this guide

    (a) Nested queries

    A complete SELECT block inside another query (in WHERE, FROM, SELECT or HAVING). Options: v IN (Q) / NOT IN; v op ANY|SOME|ALL (Q) with op in {=,<>,<,<=,>,>=} (= ANY is IN); EXISTS (Q) / NOT EXISTS; UNIQUE (Q) (no duplicate rows); a scalar subquery returning one value; tuple comparison (Pno, Hours) IN (…). A correlated nested query refers to the outer tuple and is (conceptually) re-evaluated for each outer tuple. Useful for queries that compare with values that must first be fetched, and for “for all” / “not any” queries.

    Nested query with ALL
    SELECT Lname, Fname FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = 5);  -- Wallace, Borg

    (b) Joined tables and outer joins

    A join written in FROM, separating join conditions from selection conditions: [INNER] JOIN … ON, NATURAL JOIN (equality on same-named attributes, rename with AS if needed), LEFT|RIGHT|FULL [OUTER] JOIN (keep unmatched tuples of the left/right/both sides, padded with NULLs), CROSS JOIN; joins may be nested. Useful for readability and for keeping tuples that have no match.

    Left outer join
    SELECT E.Lname AS Employee_name, S.Lname AS Supervisor_name
FROM   EMPLOYEE AS E LEFT OUTER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS S ON E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn;
-- 8 rows; Borg appears with Supervisor_name = NULL (an inner join gives 7)

    (c) Aggregate functions and grouping

    COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX (with optional DISTINCT) summarise a collection of values; GROUP BY partitions tuples into groups and applies them per group; HAVING filters groups. Useful for summary reports (per department, per project). Example: SELECT Dno, COUNT(*), AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno gives (1, 1, 55000), (4, 3, 31000), (5, 4, 33250). Rule: every non-aggregated SELECT column must be a grouping attribute.

    (d) Triggers

    An active rule of the form Event–Condition–Action (ECA). Options: BEFORE | AFTER (or INSTEAD OF); events INSERT | UPDATE [OF cols] | DELETE ON table; granularity FOR EACH ROW (row-level, can use NEW/OLD) or statement-level; optional WHEN condition; action = SQL statements or a procedure call. Useful for monitoring, maintaining derived data, enforcing complex rules, notification.

    Trigger R5
    CREATE TRIGGER SALARY_VIOLATION
BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF Salary, Super_ssn ON EMPLOYEE
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN (NEW.Salary > (SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Ssn = NEW.Super_ssn))
     INFORM_SUPERVISOR(NEW.Super_ssn, NEW.Ssn);

    (e) Assertions, and how they differ from triggers

    CREATE ASSERTION name CHECK (condition) states a general constraint that must be true in every database state; usually written as NOT EXISTS (query that finds violating tuples). The DBMS rejects any update that would violate it.

    Assertion
    CREATE ASSERTION SALARY_CONSTRAINT
CHECK ( NOT EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE E, EMPLOYEE M, DEPARTMENT D
                     WHERE E.Salary > M.Salary AND E.Dno = D.Dnumber
                       AND D.Mgr_ssn = M.Ssn ) );
    AssertionTrigger
    NatureDeclarative: what must always holdProcedural: what to do when an event happens
    When checkedOn every relevant change (DBMS decides)Only on the listed events, before/after them
    On violationUpdate is rejectedAny action: fix data, log, notify, call a procedure, or reject
    UseIntegrity constraints spanning tablesMonitoring, derived data, alerts, custom handling

    (Attribute/tuple CHECK constraints are checked only on insert/update of that table; assertions are for constraints that cannot be stated that way.)

    (f) The WITH clause

    Defines a temporary named table used only in this one query (like a view that is dropped afterwards); WITH RECURSIVE allows recursive queries (e.g. all supervisees at every level). Useful to break a complex query into readable named steps and to reuse an intermediate result.

    WITH clause
    WITH DEPT_AVG (Dno, Avg_sal) AS
     ( SELECT Dno, AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno )
SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname, E.Salary
FROM   EMPLOYEE E JOIN DEPT_AVG A ON E.Dno = A.Dno
WHERE  E.Salary > A.Avg_sal;            -- Wong, Wallace, Narayan

    (g) The CASE construct

    Returns a value chosen by conditions: CASE WHEN c1 THEN v1 WHEN c2 THEN v2 … [ELSE v] END (simple form: CASE expr WHEN val THEN …); missing ELSE gives NULL. It can be used wherever a value is expected: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, inside aggregates, INSERT and UPDATE.

    CASE in UPDATE (U6 prime)
    UPDATE EMPLOYEE
SET    Salary = CASE WHEN Dno = 5 THEN Salary + 2000
                     WHEN Dno = 4 THEN Salary + 1500
                     WHEN Dno = 1 THEN Salary + 3000
                     ELSE Salary + 0 END;

    (h) Views and their updatability

    CREATE VIEW name [(cols)] AS SELECT … defines a virtual table derived from base tables (DROP VIEW removes it). Useful to simplify frequent queries, and for security (show only some rows/columns). Implemented by query modification (rewrite the view query into a query on base tables) or view materialisation (store the result, keep it up to date by immediate, lazy or periodic update). Updatability: queries on a view are always allowed; updates only when they map to exactly one update on the base tables:

    • single-table view with no aggregates, containing the primary key and all NOT NULL columns without defaults: updatable;
    • views on several tables with joins: generally not updatable (ambiguous mapping);
    • views with grouping or aggregate functions: not updatable.

    WITH CHECK OPTION makes the DBMS reject view updates whose rows would not satisfy the view’s condition.

    (i) Schema change commands

    DROP SCHEMA|TABLE name CASCADE|RESTRICT (RESTRICT: only if nothing references it; CASCADE: also drop referencing constraints and views); ALTER TABLE to ADD COLUMN (new column is NULL unless a DEFAULT is given, so NOT NULL is not allowed without a default), DROP COLUMN … CASCADE|RESTRICT, ALTER COLUMN … SET DEFAULT | DROP DEFAULT, ADD CONSTRAINT / DROP CONSTRAINT name (constraint must be named). Useful for schema evolution while the database is in use.

    Schema changes
    ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN Job VARCHAR(12);
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.DEPARTMENT ALTER COLUMN Mgr_ssn SET DEFAULT '333445555';
ALTER TABLE COMPANY.EMPLOYEE DROP CONSTRAINT EMPSUPERFK CASCADE;
    7.5COMPANY grouping queriesE&N Ex. 7.5 · p. 236

    Specify the following queries on the database in Figure 5.5 in SQL. Show the query results if each query is applied to the database state in Figure 5.6.

    1. For each department whose average employee salary is more than $30,000, retrieve the department name and the number of employees working for that department.
    2. Suppose that we want the number of male employees in each department making more than $30,000, rather than all employees (as in Exercise 7.5a). Can we specify this query in SQL? Why or why not?
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Ssn is the key of EMPLOYEE and Dnumber of DEPARTMENT, so COUNT(*) in a department group counts each employee once. Why: Figure 5.5 underlines them.
    2. Dno and Salary are never NULL. Why: every employee in Figure 5.6 has both (Dno is NOT NULL in Figure 6.1). If a Salary were NULL, AVG would ignore it but COUNT(*) would still count the employee, which is what “number of employees” means.
    3. Departments with no employees are not listed: their average salary is undefined (NULL), so they cannot satisfy “average >>> 30,000”.

    (a)

    7.5(a)
    SELECT   Dname, COUNT(*) AS Num_employees
FROM     DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
WHERE    Dnumber = Dno                 -- join: each employee with his/her department
GROUP BY Dname                         -- one group per department (Dname is UNIQUE)
HAVING   AVG(Salary) > 30000;          -- condition on the group, so HAVING not WHERE
    • FROM/WHERE pair every employee with the department he/she works for (8 rows).
    • GROUP BY Dname forms one group per department. Grouping by Dnumber, Dname is equally correct.
    • HAVING keeps the department only if the average over all its employees exceeds 30,000; the condition uses an aggregate, so it cannot be in WHERE.
    • SELECT outputs the name and the group size.

    Group values (verified): dept 1: 1 employee, avg 55000; dept 4: 3 employees, avg 93000/3 = 31000; dept 5: 4 employees, avg 133000/4 = 33250. All three exceed 30,000.

    DnameNum_employees
    Research4
    Administration3
    Headquarters1

    (b)

    Reading. “Making more than $30,000” refers to the department’s average salary as in 7.5a (that is what “rather than all employees (as in 7.5a)” changes): for each department whose average salary over all employees is >>> 30,000, count only its male employees.

    Answer: yes, but not by adding Sex = ’M’ to the WHERE clause of 7.5a. WHERE is applied before grouping, so it would remove the female employees before AVG is computed; the HAVING test would then use the average of the male salaries only, which is a different condition:

    7.5(b): wrong attempt
    -- WRONG: the average is now computed over male employees only
SELECT Dname, COUNT(*) FROM DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Dnumber = Dno AND Sex = 'M'
GROUP BY Dname HAVING AVG(Salary) > 30000;
-- gives Research 3, Headquarters 1: Administration is lost, because its only
-- male (Jabbar, 25000) has average 25000, although the department average is 31000.

    The two conditions need two different sets of tuples (all employees for the average, male employees for the count), so a single grouping cannot do both. We use a nested query to choose the departments:

    7.5(b): nested query
    SELECT   Dname, COUNT(*) AS Num_male
FROM     DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
WHERE    Dnumber = Dno AND Sex = 'M'           -- count only male employees
  AND    Dno IN ( SELECT   Dno                  -- departments whose average over
                  FROM     EMPLOYEE             -- ALL employees is > 30000
                  GROUP BY Dno
                  HAVING   AVG(Salary) > 30000 )
GROUP BY Dname;

    Alternative without nesting: count conditionally inside the group, so the average still uses all rows:

    7.5(b): conditional count
    SELECT   Dname, COUNT(CASE WHEN Sex = 'M' THEN 1 END) AS Num_male  -- CASE gives NULL for females
FROM     DEPARTMENT, EMPLOYEE
WHERE    Dnumber = Dno
GROUP BY Dname
HAVING   AVG(Salary) > 30000;

    Both give (verified):

    DnameNum_male
    Research3 (Smith, Wong, Narayan)
    Administration1 (Jabbar)
    Headquarters1 (Borg)

    (The nested version omits a qualifying department that has no male employees; the CASE version lists it with 0. No such department exists here.)

    Other reading. If “making more than $30,000” describes the male employees (count males earning over 30,000 in each department with average >>> 30,000), add AND Salary > 30000 next to Sex = ’M’ in the nested version: result Research 2 (Wong, Narayan), Headquarters 1 (Borg) (verified).

    Answer

    (a) Research 4, Administration 3, Headquarters 1. (b) Yes, it can be specified, but only with a nested query (or a conditional count): putting Sex=’M’ in WHERE filters the tuples before AVG is computed, so the average would be over male salaries only and Administration would wrongly disappear. Correct result: Research 3, Administration 1, Headquarters 1.

    What the grader checks
    • Aggregate condition in HAVING, not WHERE (WHERE AVG(Salary) > 30000 is illegal).
    • Every non-aggregated SELECT column (Dname) is in GROUP BY.
    • 7.5b: explain why the simple version fails (WHERE acts before grouping and changes the average); “No, it cannot be done” without the nested query loses marks, as does adding Sex=’M’ to WHERE.
    • Results shown on Figure 5.6 (the question asks for them), with the arithmetic of the averages.
    7.6UNIVERSITY: straight-A studentsE&N Ex. 7.6 · p. 237

    Specify the following queries in SQL on the database schema in Figure 1.2.

    1. Retrieve the names and major departments of all straight-A students (students who have a grade of A in all their courses).
    2. Retrieve the names and major departments of all students who do not have a grade of A in any of their courses.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Student_number is the key of STUDENT; Name is not (two students may share a name). Why: Figure 2.1/1.2; so we test grades by Student_number, not by Name.
    2. “All their courses” = all their rows in GRADE_REPORT (each row is a section the student took). Why: grades are stored only there.
    3. In (a), a student with no grades is not straight-A. Why: “for all” over an empty set is vacuously true, but nobody would call a student with no courses straight-A; we therefore require at least one grade. (Dropping the EXISTS line gives the vacuous reading.)
    4. In (b), a student with no grades is listed (he has no A in any course). Grade is never NULL (all are filled in Figure 1.2); a NULL grade (course in progress) would count as “not A” in (a) through <> ’A’ being UNKNOWN, see the remark below.

    (a) Straight-A students: “there is no course in which the grade is not A”

    7.6(a): NOT EXISTS
    SELECT Name, Major
FROM   STUDENT S
WHERE  EXISTS     ( SELECT * FROM GRADE_REPORT G          -- has at least one grade
                    WHERE  G.Student_number = S.Student_number )
  AND  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM GRADE_REPORT G          -- and no non-A grade
                    WHERE  G.Student_number = S.Student_number
                      AND  G.Grade <> 'A' );
    • The outer query takes each student once (no join, so no duplicates).
    • The first correlated subquery checks that the student took at least one course (Assumption A3).
    • The second correlated subquery looks for a counterexample: a grade of this student that is not A. “All are A” ≡\equiv≡ “no grade is not A”.

    Alternative with grouping (count all grades and count the A grades; they must be equal):

    7.6(a): grouping
    SELECT   S.Name, S.Major
FROM     STUDENT S JOIN GRADE_REPORT G ON S.Student_number = G.Student_number
GROUP BY S.Student_number, S.Name, S.Major       -- group by the key, not by Name
HAVING   COUNT(*) = COUNT(CASE WHEN G.Grade = 'A' THEN 1 END);

    (The inner join already drops students without grades. With a NULL grade, COUNT(*) counts it but the CASE does not, so such a student is excluded, which matches the NOT EXISTS version only if we write G.Grade <> ’A’ OR G.Grade IS NULL there.)

    Result on Figure 1.2: empty. Smith (17) has B and C; Brown (8) has A, A, B, A: the B in section 102 (CS3320) disqualifies him. (Check: if that B were an A, both versions return (Brown, CS); verified.)

    NameMajor
    (no rows)

    (b) Students with no A at all

    7.6(b): NOT EXISTS
    SELECT Name, Major
FROM   STUDENT S
WHERE  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT * FROM GRADE_REPORT G
                    WHERE  G.Student_number = S.Student_number
                      AND  G.Grade = 'A' );       -- no A grade exists for S

    Equivalent with NOT IN (safe here because Student_number in GRADE_REPORT is part of the key, so it is never NULL):

    7.6(b): NOT IN
    SELECT Name, Major FROM STUDENT
WHERE  Student_number NOT IN ( SELECT Student_number FROM GRADE_REPORT
                               WHERE  Grade = 'A' );

    Result on Figure 1.2 (verified, all versions):

    NameMajor
    SmithCS
    Answer

    (a) NOT EXISTS a non-A grade (plus at least one grade): result empty on Figure 1.2. (b) NOT EXISTS an A grade: result (Smith, CS).

    What the grader checks
    • (a) is a “for all” query: it needs NOT EXISTS (… <> ’A’), a count comparison, or division. WHERE Grade = ’A’ with a join is the classic wrong answer: it lists every student with some A (Brown would appear).
    • (b) WHERE Grade <> ’A’ with a join is wrong the same way (lists students with some non-A grade: Brown and Smith).
    • Grouping by Name only (not the key) merges different students with the same name.
    • State what happens to students with no grades in each part; NOT IN is safe only if the subquery column cannot be NULL.
    7.7COMPANY: nested queriesE&N Ex. 7.7 · p. 237★ Must-do

    In SQL, specify the following queries on the database in Figure 5.5 using the concept of nested queries and other concepts described in this chapter.

    1. Retrieve the names of all employees who work in the department that has the employee with the highest salary among all employees.
    2. Retrieve the names of all employees whose supervisor’s supervisor has ‘888665555’ for Ssn.
    3. Retrieve the names of employees who make at least $10,000 more than the employee who is paid the least in the company.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Salary and Dno are never NULL. Why: true in Figure 5.6; MAX/MIN ignore NULLs anyway, and Dno is NOT NULL in Figure 6.1.
    2. (a) Ties: if several employees share the highest salary and are in different departments, we list the employees of all those departments. Why: the question says “the department” (assumes one), and with ties each such department “has the employee with the highest salary”. This is why we use IN, not =: with = a tie across departments would make the subquery return several rows and the query would fail. We do not use ORDER BY … LIMIT 1, which silently drops ties.
    3. (c) “At least $10,000 more” means Salary≥min⁡+10000\text{Salary} \ge \min + 10000Salary≥min+10000 (inclusive). The least-paid employee may be one of several with the same minimum salary; only the value matters.
    4. “Names” = Fname and Lname.

    (a) Employees of the department of the top earner

    7.7(a)
    SELECT Fname, Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Dno IN ( SELECT Dno                          -- department(s) of the top earner(s)
                FROM   EMPLOYEE
                WHERE  Salary = ( SELECT MAX(Salary)  -- the highest salary: 55000
                                  FROM   EMPLOYEE ) );
    • Innermost query: the highest salary in the company (55000).
    • Middle query: the Dno of every employee earning that salary (Borg →\rightarrow→ 1).
    • Outer query: every employee whose Dno is in that set.

    Alternative with >= ALL: WHERE Dno IN (SELECT Dno FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Salary >= ALL (SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE)).

    Result (verified): department 1 has only Borg.

    FnameLname
    JamesBorg

    (b) Supervisor’s supervisor is 888665555

    7.7(b)
    SELECT Fname, Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Super_ssn IN ( SELECT Ssn                       -- my supervisor is one of the
                      FROM   EMPLOYEE                  -- employees directly
                      WHERE  Super_ssn = '888665555' ); -- supervised by 888665555

    The nested query finds the employees whose supervisor is 888665555 (Wong 333445555 and Wallace 987654321); the outer query returns the employees supervised by one of them. Equivalent self-join: SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname FROM EMPLOYEE E, EMPLOYEE S WHERE E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn AND S.Super_ssn = ’888665555’;

    Result (verified):

    FnameLname(supervisor)
    JohnSmithWong
    AliciaZelayaWallace
    RameshNarayanWong
    JoyceEnglishWong
    AhmadJabbarWallace

    (c) At least $10,000 more than the lowest-paid employee

    7.7(c)
    SELECT Fname, Lname
FROM   EMPLOYEE
WHERE  Salary >= 10000 + ( SELECT MIN(Salary)    -- lowest salary: 25000
                           FROM   EMPLOYEE );

    The scalar nested query returns one value (25000), so the condition is Salary ≥\ge≥ 35000. Alternative: WHERE Salary - 10000 >= SOME (SELECT Salary FROM EMPLOYEE): it is true exactly when Salary −-− 10000 is at least some salary, i.e. at least the minimum. Writing >= ALL there would be wrong: it compares with the maximum salary.

    Result (verified):

    FnameLnameSalary
    FranklinWong40000
    JenniferWallace43000
    RameshNarayan38000
    JamesBorg55000
    Answer

    (a) James Borg. (b) Smith, Zelaya, Narayan, English, Jabbar. (c) Wong, Wallace, Narayan, Borg (salary ≥\ge≥ 35000).

    What the grader checks
    • The question asks for nested queries: use them (a join answer to (b) is a fine extra, not a replacement).
    • (a) ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 1 loses ties; Dno = (subquery) fails if the subquery returns several rows; WHERE Salary = MAX(Salary) (aggregate in WHERE without a subquery) is illegal.
    • (b) Direction of the supervision: “my supervisor’s supervisor” means E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn AND S.Super_ssn = ’888665555’; reversing it returns Borg’s supervisees’ bosses instead.
    • (c) >= vs > (“at least”), and ALL instead of SOME/MIN compares with the maximum.
    7.8Views on COMPANYE&N Ex. 7.8 · p. 237

    Specify the following views in SQL on the COMPANY database schema shown in Figure 5.5.

    1. A view that has the department name, manager name, and manager salary for every department
    2. A view that has the employee name, supervisor name, and employee salary for each employee who works in the ‘Research’ department
    3. A view that has the project name, controlling department name, number of employees, and total hours worked per week on the project for each project
    4. A view that has the project name, controlling department name, number of employees, and total hours worked per week on the project for each project with more than one employee working on it
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Name” of a person = first and last name, kept as two columns (Fname, Lname). Why: that is how EMPLOYEE stores it; concatenating is also acceptable.
    2. (b) An employee of Research with no supervisor is still listed, with NULL supervisor name (LEFT OUTER JOIN). Why: “for each employee who works in Research”. In Figure 5.6 every Research employee has a supervisor, so the result is the same with an inner join.
    3. (c) “Number of employees” = number of WORKS_ON rows of the project. Why: (Essn, Pno) is the key of WORKS_ON, so each employee is counted once per project. A project with no workers is still shown, with 0 and NULL hours (LEFT OUTER JOIN and COUNT(W.Essn), not COUNT(*)).
    4. (c), (d) Total hours = SUM(Hours); a NULL Hours (Borg on project 20) is ignored by SUM, but Borg is still counted as an employee.
    5. Group by Pnumber (the key) as well as Pname, Dname, so two projects with the same name could not be merged.

    (a)

    7.8(a)
    CREATE VIEW DEPT_MGR (Dname, Mgr_fname, Mgr_lname, Mgr_salary) AS
SELECT D.Dname, E.Fname, E.Lname, E.Salary
FROM   DEPARTMENT D JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON D.Mgr_ssn = E.Ssn;   -- the manager's tuple

    Join on Mgr_ssn = Ssn (not Dno = Dnumber, which would give all employees). Mgr_ssn is NOT NULL, so every department appears.

    DnameMgr_fnameMgr_lnameMgr_salary
    ResearchFranklinWong40000
    AdministrationJenniferWallace43000
    HeadquartersJamesBorg55000

    (b)

    7.8(b)
    CREATE VIEW RESEARCH_EMP (Emp_fname, Emp_lname, Sup_fname, Sup_lname, Emp_salary) AS
SELECT E.Fname, E.Lname, S.Fname, S.Lname, E.Salary
FROM   (EMPLOYEE E JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON E.Dno = D.Dnumber)     -- employee's department
       LEFT OUTER JOIN EMPLOYEE S ON E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn       -- supervisor (may be NULL)
WHERE  D.Dname = 'Research';

    Two tuple variables over EMPLOYEE are needed: E for the employee, S for the supervisor. Column names must be given in the view header because Fname/Lname occur twice.

    Emp_fnameEmp_lnameSup_fnameSup_lnameEmp_salary
    JohnSmithFranklinWong30000
    FranklinWongJamesBorg40000
    RameshNarayanFranklinWong38000
    JoyceEnglishFranklinWong25000

    (c)

    7.8(c)
    CREATE VIEW PROJ_SUMMARY (Pname, Dname, Num_emps, Total_hours) AS
SELECT   P.Pname, D.Dname, COUNT(W.Essn), SUM(W.Hours)
FROM     (PROJECT P JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON P.Dnum = D.Dnumber)  -- controlling department
         LEFT OUTER JOIN WORKS_ON W ON W.Pno = P.Pnumber      -- keep projects with no workers
GROUP BY P.Pnumber, P.Pname, D.Dname;

    (d)

    7.8(d)
    CREATE VIEW BIG_PROJ_SUMMARY (Pname, Dname, Num_emps, Total_hours) AS
SELECT   P.Pname, D.Dname, COUNT(*), SUM(W.Hours)
FROM     PROJECT P, DEPARTMENT D, WORKS_ON W
WHERE    P.Dnum = D.Dnumber AND W.Pno = P.Pnumber
GROUP BY P.Pnumber, P.Pname, D.Dname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 1;                  -- condition on the group: more than one employee

    (Here an inner join is fine: a project with no worker cannot have more than one. Equivalently: SELECT * FROM PROJ_SUMMARY WHERE Num_emps > 1.)

    Contents on Figure 5.6 (verified). Every project has at least two workers, so (c) and (d) contain the same six rows:

    PnameDnameNum_empsTotal_hours
    ProductXResearch252.5
    ProductYResearch337.5
    ProductZResearch250.0
    ComputerizationAdministration355.0
    ReorganizationHeadquarters325.0
    NewbenefitsAdministration355.0

    Reorganization: Wong 10 + Wallace 15 + Borg NULL gives 3 employees but 25.0 hours (SUM ignores the NULL).

    What the grader checks
    • (a) join on Mgr_ssn = Ssn; (b) two aliases of EMPLOYEE with the correct direction E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn.
    • (c) after a LEFT OUTER JOIN use COUNT(W.Essn): COUNT(*) counts the NULL-padded row and gives 1 for a project with no workers.
    • (d) “more than one employee” is a group condition: HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, not WHERE.
    • GROUP BY must include every non-aggregated output column (Pname, Dname).
    7.9Queries and updates on the DEPT_SUMMARY viewE&N Ex. 7.9 · p. 237★ Must-do

    Consider the following view, DEPT_SUMMARY, defined on the COMPANY database in Figure 5.6:

    View definition
    CREATE VIEW DEPT_SUMMARY (D, C, Total_s, Average_s)
AS SELECT   Dno, COUNT (*), SUM (Salary), AVG (Salary)
   FROM     EMPLOYEE
   GROUP BY Dno;

    State which of the following queries and updates would be allowed on the view. If a query or update would be allowed, show what the corresponding query or update on the base relations would look like, and give its result when applied to the database in Figure 5.6.

    Statements (a) to (e)
    a. SELECT * FROM DEPT_SUMMARY;
b. SELECT D, C FROM DEPT_SUMMARY WHERE TOTAL_S > 100000;
c. SELECT D, AVERAGE_S FROM DEPT_SUMMARY
   WHERE  C > ( SELECT C FROM DEPT_SUMMARY WHERE D = 4 );
d. UPDATE DEPT_SUMMARY SET D = 3 WHERE D = 4;
e. DELETE FROM DEPT_SUMMARY WHERE C > 4;
    Solution · written for this guide

    Principle. Any query on a view is allowed: the DBMS uses query modification, replacing each view column by its defining expression (D →\rightarrow→ Dno, C →\rightarrow→ COUNT(*), Total_s →\rightarrow→ SUM(Salary), Average_s →\rightarrow→ AVG(Salary)) and adding the view’s FROM and GROUP BY. A condition on a view column that is an aggregate becomes a HAVING condition on the base table. An update on this view is not allowed, because the view is defined with grouping and aggregate functions: each view row summarises many base rows, so no unique update of EMPLOYEE corresponds to the change.

    The view contents on Figure 5.6 (verified):

    DCTotal_sAverage_s
    115500055000
    439300031000
    5413300033250

    (a) Allowed.

    Modified query and result:

    7.9(a) on base table
    SELECT   Dno, COUNT(*), SUM(Salary), AVG(Salary)
FROM     EMPLOYEE
GROUP BY Dno;

    Result: the whole table above (3 rows).

    (b) Allowed.

    The condition on Total_s is a condition on SUM(Salary), so it moves to HAVING:

    7.9(b) on base table
    SELECT   Dno, COUNT(*)
FROM     EMPLOYEE
GROUP BY Dno
HAVING   SUM(Salary) > 100000;

    Only department 5 has a total above 100000 (133000).

    DC
    54

    (c) Allowed.

    Both the outer view reference and the nested one are modified:

    7.9(c) on base table
    SELECT   Dno, AVG(Salary)
FROM     EMPLOYEE
GROUP BY Dno
HAVING   COUNT(*) > ( SELECT COUNT(*)          -- C of department 4
                      FROM   EMPLOYEE
                      WHERE  Dno = 4 );         -- (= ... GROUP BY Dno HAVING Dno = 4)

    Department 4 has 3 employees; only department 5 has more than 3 (4).

    DAverage_s
    533250

    (d) Not allowed.

    D is the grouping attribute; the view row (4, 3, 93000, 31000) is derived from the three EMPLOYEE tuples of department 4. The update could only be realised by changing the Dno of all employees of department 4 to 3 (UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Dno = 3 WHERE Dno = 4), but the view gives no way to decide this: it is not a one-to-one mapping from view rows to base rows, and SQL does not allow updates on views with GROUP BY/aggregates. (Here it would also violate referential integrity: there is no department 3 in DEPARTMENT.) The DBMS rejects the statement.

    (e) Not allowed.

    C is COUNT(*), a computed aggregate. Deleting a view row would require deleting some set of EMPLOYEE tuples so that the group disappears or its count drops; which tuples (all employees of the department? enough to make C ≤\le≤ 4?) is ambiguous, so the update cannot be translated uniquely and is rejected for an aggregate view. (On Figure 5.6 no department has C >>> 4, so even a hypothetical translation would delete nothing; the statement is still illegal because the decision is made from the view definition, not from the current data.)

    Answer

    (a), (b), (c) are allowed (queries, translated by query modification; aggregate conditions become HAVING). Results: (a) the 3-row view; (b) (5, 4); (c) (5, 33250). (d) and (e) are not allowed: DEPT_SUMMARY uses GROUP BY and aggregates, so a view update has no unique translation to updates on EMPLOYEE.

    What the grader checks
    • For each allowed query the modified base-table query must be shown, not only the result.
    • The view’s aggregate columns in a WHERE condition must become HAVING conditions; writing WHERE SUM(Salary) > 100000 is illegal.
    • (c): the nested reference to the view must be modified too.
    • (d), (e): “not allowed” needs the reason (aggregate/grouped view: no unique mapping to base tuples). Saying “allowed, no rows affected” for (e) is the common wrong answer.

    17  Chapter 10 exercise

    Textbook exercises

    10.7Embedded SQL in C: a student’s GPAE&N Ex. 10.7 · p. 340

    Consider the database shown in Figure 1.2, whose schema is shown in Figure 2.1. Write a program segment to read a student’s name and print his or her grade point average, assuming that A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, and D = 1 points. Use embedded SQL with C as the host language.

    Schema (Figure 2.1): STUDENT(Name, Student_number, Class, Major); COURSE(Course_name, Course_number, Credit_hours, Department); PREREQUISITE(Course_number, Prerequisite_number); SECTION(Section_identifier, Course_number, Semester, Year, Instructor); GRADE_REPORT(Student_number, Section_identifier, Grade).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. GPA is weighted by credit hours: GPA =∑(points×Credit_hours)/∑Credit_hours= \sum(\text{points}\times\text{Credit\_hours}) / \sum \text{Credit\_hours}=∑(points×Credit_hours)/∑Credit_hours. Why: this is the usual definition, and COURSE stores Credit_hours (reached via SECTION). The simple average of the points is a valid reading too; the change is one line (shown below).
    2. Name is not a key: several students can have the same name. Why: Student_number is the key of STUDENT. So the program loops over all students with that name and prints a GPA for each, with the student number. (Using SELECT … INTO for the student number would fail with more than one match.)
    3. Grades other than A–D (e.g. F) earn 0 points but their credit hours count; a NULL grade (course not finished) is skipped. A student with no graded courses has no GPA (avoid division by zero).
    4. A connection to the UNIVERSITY database is already open, as in the book’s examples; prompt and printf are used as in Figures 10.2–10.3.

    Program segment

    EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE SECTION ;
  varchar sname [16] ;               /* name read from the user           */
  int     snum ;                     /* Student_number of one match       */
  char    grade [2] ;                /* one grade, e.g. "A"               */
  int     credits ;                  /* Credit_hours of that course       */
  int     SQLCODE ; char SQLSTATE [6] ;
EXEC SQL END DECLARE SECTION ;
int   points, total_points, total_credits, found ;

prompt("Enter the student's name: ", sname) ;

EXEC SQL DECLARE STU CURSOR FOR          /* all students with this name   */
  SELECT Student_number FROM STUDENT WHERE Name = :sname ;

EXEC SQL DECLARE GRD CURSOR FOR          /* grades + credits of student   */
  SELECT G.Grade, C.Credit_hours
  FROM   GRADE_REPORT G, SECTION S, COURSE C
  WHERE  G.Student_number     = :snum
    AND  G.Section_identifier = S.Section_identifier
    AND  S.Course_number      = C.Course_number
    AND  G.Grade IS NOT NULL ;

found = 0 ;
EXEC SQL OPEN STU ;
EXEC SQL FETCH FROM STU INTO :snum ;
while (SQLCODE == 0) {                   /* one iteration per student     */
  found = 1 ;
  total_points = 0 ; total_credits = 0 ;
  EXEC SQL OPEN GRD ;                    /* query runs with current :snum */
  EXEC SQL FETCH FROM GRD INTO :grade, :credits ;
  while (SQLCODE == 0) {                 /* one iteration per grade       */
    switch (grade[0]) {
      case 'A': points = 4 ; break ;
      case 'B': points = 3 ; break ;
      case 'C': points = 2 ; break ;
      case 'D': points = 1 ; break ;
      default : points = 0 ;             /* F or any other grade          */
    }
    total_points  += points * credits ;
    total_credits += credits ;
    EXEC SQL FETCH FROM GRD INTO :grade, :credits ;
  }
  if (SQLCODE < 0) printf("Database error EXEC SQL CLOSE GRD ;
  if (total_credits > 0)
    printf("Student (float) total_points / total_credits) ;
  else
    printf("Student EXEC SQL FETCH FROM STU INTO :snum ;
}
if (SQLCODE < 0)  printf("Database error else if (!found)  printf("No student named EXEC SQL CLOSE STU ;

    How it works

    • Declare section: the shared (host) variables used inside SQL statements, prefixed by : there. Their C types match the SQL types (string one character longer for the terminating \ 0). SQLCODE/SQLSTATE are the communication variables. Variables used only in C (points, totals) are declared outside.
    • Cursor STU loops over every student with the given name (Assumption A2). OPEN runs the query; each FETCH copies the next row into :snum.
    • Cursor GRD joins GRADE_REPORT →\rightarrow→ SECTION →\rightarrow→ COURSE to get each grade with the course’s credit hours. It is opened once per student, so it uses the current value of :snum; it is closed before being reopened.
    • Loop termination / error checks: SQLCODE = 0 means a row was fetched, SQLCODE = 100 (SQLSTATE ’02000’) means no more rows, SQLCODE < 0 means an error. Each loop stops on anything other than 0, and the error case is reported separately from “no more rows”.
    • The point mapping A=4, …, D=1 is done in C; the GPA is printed only if the student has graded credit hours.

    For the unweighted reading (simple average of points per course), replace points * credits by points and credits by 1 in the two sums.

    Alternative: let SQL compute the GPA (one row per student)

    The point mapping can be done with CASE and the averaging with aggregates, so each fetch returns the finished GPA:

    GPA computed in SQL
    EXEC SQL DECLARE GPA CURSOR FOR
  SELECT ST.Student_number,
         SUM( CASE G.Grade WHEN 'A' THEN 4 WHEN 'B' THEN 3
                           WHEN 'C' THEN 2 WHEN 'D' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
              * C.Credit_hours ) * 1.0 / SUM(C.Credit_hours)
  FROM   STUDENT ST, GRADE_REPORT G, SECTION S, COURSE C
  WHERE  ST.Name = :sname
    AND  ST.Student_number = G.Student_number
    AND  G.Section_identifier = S.Section_identifier
    AND  S.Course_number = C.Course_number
    AND  G.Grade IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY ST.Student_number ;
-- then: OPEN GPA; FETCH GPA INTO :snum, :gpa; while (SQLCODE == 0) {print; FETCH};
-- CLOSE GPA.  (The * 1.0 avoids integer division.)

    Check on Figure 1.2 (verified with SQLite)

    InputGraded courses (grade, credit hours)Weighted GPAUnweighted
    Smith (17)MATH2410 B (3), CS1310 C (4)(9+8)/7=2.43(9+8)/7 = 2.43(9+8)/7=2.432.502.502.50
    Brown (8)MATH2410 A (3), CS1310 A (4), CS3320 B (4), CS3380 A (3)(12+16+12+12)/14=3.71(12+16+12+12)/14 = 3.71(12+16+12+12)/14=3.713.753.753.75
    Jonesnone: “No student named Jones”––
    Answer

    Read the name into a host variable; loop with a cursor over the students with that name; for each, loop with a second cursor over (Grade, Credit_hours) from GRADE_REPORT ⋈\bowtie⋈ SECTION ⋈\bowtie⋈ COURSE, map A/B/C/D to 4/3/2/1, accumulate, and print ∑\sum∑points×\times×credits / ∑/\ \sum/ ∑credits. Smith: 2.43, Brown: 3.71.

    What the grader checks
    • Host variables declared in BEGIN/END DECLARE SECTION and prefixed with : inside SQL.
    • A cursor (DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH in a loop, CLOSE) for the multi-row grade result; SELECT … INTO works only for single-row results.
    • Loop controlled by SQLCODE (0 = row, 100 = no more data, <<<0 = error) or SQLSTATE ’02000’.
    • Correct join path GRADE_REPORT →\rightarrow→ SECTION →\rightarrow→ COURSE if credit hours are used; state whether the GPA is weighted.
    • Handle the name not found / no grades (division by zero).

    18  Exam cheat sheet

    SQL at a glance

    • Declarative, based on TRC. Table = multiset (unless key/DISTINCT); rows unordered.
    • Written: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Evaluated: FROM →\to→ WHERE →\to→ GROUP BY →\to→ HAVING →\to→ SELECT (DISTINCT) →\to→ ORDER BY. Hence: no aggregate in WHERE; SELECT alias not in WHERE (OK in ORDER BY); non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY; only ORDER BY gives an order.

    DDL and constraints

    • Column: col TYPE [NOT NULL] [DEFAULT v] [CHECK (c)]; no DEFAULT ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ NULL. Types INT, DECIMAL(i,j), CHAR(n), VARCHAR(n), DATE; CREATE DOMAIN D AS CHAR(9).
    • Table: PRIMARY KEY(A,B) (one, implies NOT NULL), UNIQUE(A), tuple CHECK, CONSTRAINT name (so it can be dropped). Composite FK = one constraint over all columns.
    CREATE TABLE ADMISSION
( Adm_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Pat_id INT NOT NULL,
  Doc_id INT,                  -- nullable: SET NULL
  Status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'Admitted'
         CHECK (Status IN ('Admitted','Discharged')),
  Adm_date DATE NOT NULL,  Dis_date DATE,
  CHECK (Dis_date IS NULL OR Dis_date >= Adm_date),
  CONSTRAINT ADM_PAT FOREIGN KEY (Pat_id) REFERENCES
    PATIENT(Pat_id) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT ADM_DOC FOREIGN KEY (Doc_id) REFERENCES
    DOCTOR(Doc_id) ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE);
    • Referential actions (on parent delete / key update): default RESTRICT/NO ACTION = reject; SET NULL (FK nullable, not in PK); SET DEFAULT (default must be valid); CASCADE (delete children / copy new key). A bad child insert is always rejected.
    • Choose: CASCADE for weak, relationship, multivalued tables; SET NULL for optional links (Super_ssn); RESTRICT when info would be lost; ON UPDATE CASCADE almost always. Cycles: add FKs later with ALTER TABLE.

    Basic queries and updates

    • No WHERE on 2 tables = Cartesian product. Same table twice needs aliases. DISTINCT is not automatic. UNION/EXCEPT/INTERSECT = sets, type-compatible; ALL versions: counts add / max⁡(0,m−n)\max(0,m-n)max(0,m−n) / min⁡(m,n)\min(m,n)min(m,n). LIKE: % any string, _ one char; BETWEEN inclusive; ORDER BY default ASC.
    • INSERT … SELECT is a snapshot; DELETE FROM T keeps the table; SET c = c*1.1 uses the old value; one table per statement.

    NULL and three-valued logic

    ANDTFU
    TTFU
    FFFF
    UUFU
    ORTFU
    TTTT
    FTFU
    UTUU
    NOT
    TF
    FT
    UU
    • Comparison with NULL = UNKNOWN; WHERE/HAVING keep only TRUE (B <> ’y’ skips NULL B). Use IS [NOT] NULL. Joins never match NULL; GROUP BY/DISTINCT put NULLs together.
    • Aggregates drop NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows. Empty: COUNT 0, others NULL. AVG = SUM/COUNT(col): (10, 15, NULL) gives COUNT(*) 3, AVG 12.5.
    • NOT IN: v NOT IN (1,2,NULL) is never TRUE ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ no rows. Use NOT EXISTS, IS NOT NULL in the subquery, or assume “never NULL”.

    Nested queries

    • IN ≡\equiv≡ = ANY; op ANY: some value (FALSE if empty); op ALL: every value (TRUE if empty); (a,b) IN (Q); [NOT] EXISTS; UNIQUE(Q); v = (Q) needs one row.
    • Correlated: inner query uses an outer alias, re-run per outer row; unqualified names bind innermost. > ALL(Q) ≡\equiv≡ > (SELECT MAX …).

    “For all” (division)

    SELECT Fname, Lname FROM EMPLOYEE      -- Q3A (safer)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  (SELECT Pnumber FROM PROJECT WHERE Dnum = 5)
  EXCEPT (SELECT Pno FROM WORKS_ON WHERE Ssn = Essn));
SELECT Lname FROM EMPLOYEE E           -- double NOT EXISTS
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM PROJECT P
  WHERE P.Dnum = 5 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM WORKS_ON W
    WHERE W.Essn = E.Ssn AND W.Pno = P.Pnumber));
    • Count form: HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT Pno) = (SELECT COUNT(*) …) on the restricted rows. Dept 5: empty; dept 4: Zelaya, Jabbar. Empty set ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ everyone.

    Joins: which rows

    [INNER] JOIN ONmatching pairs only
    NATURAL JOINequal on all same-named cols, kept once
    LEFT / RIGHT JOINinner + unmatched left / right, NULL-padded
    FULL JOINinner + unmatched of both sides
    CROSS JOIN∣R∣×∣S∣|R|\times|S|∣R∣×∣S∣
    anti-joinLEFT JOIN … WHERE B.key IS NULL
    • ∣R⟕S∣=∣R⋈S∣+#|R\mathbin{\text{⟕}} S| = |R\bowtie S| + \#∣R⟕S∣=∣R⋈S∣+#unmatched RRR; full adds both sides. FULL without FULL:
    SELECT * FROM R LEFT JOIN S ON R.B = S.B  UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM R RIGHT JOIN S ON R.B = S.B
WHERE R.A IS NULL;     -- R.A never NULL in R (key)

    (plain UNION of left and right also works but drops genuine duplicates.)

    Aggregates, GROUP BY, HAVING

    • Aggregates in SELECT/HAVING/ORDER BY, never WHERE; no nesting MAX(SUM()). SELECT/HAVING may use only grouping columns + aggregates; group by the key.
    • WHERE filters rows before grouping (changes what is counted); HAVING filters groups. Row condition →\to→ WHERE, aggregate condition →\to→ HAVING.
    • Big groups, count a subset: decide “big” on the unfiltered table: WHERE Salary > 30000 AND Dno IN (SELECT Dno FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Dno HAVING COUNT(*) > 2) GROUP BY Dno.
    • Zero counts: inner join drops empty groups; use LEFT JOIN (condition in ON) + COUNT(child.col).

    WITH, CASE, recursive

    • WITH T(c) AS (SELECT …) SELECT … FROM T: temp table for one query. CASE WHEN c1 THEN v1 … ELSE v END wherever a value goes.
    WITH RECURSIVE SUP_EMP (SupSsn, EmpSsn) AS
( SELECT Super_ssn, Ssn FROM EMPLOYEE       -- base
  WHERE Super_ssn IS NOT NULL
  UNION
  SELECT S.SupSsn, E.Ssn                    -- next level
  FROM EMPLOYEE E, SUP_EMP S WHERE E.Super_ssn = S.EmpSsn )
SELECT * FROM SUP_EMP;                      -- 12 rows

    Query patterns

    -- n-th highest distinct: exactly n-1 distinct larger
SELECT DISTINCT E1.Salary FROM EMPLOYEE E1
WHERE 3-1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT E2.Salary)
   FROM EMPLOYEE E2 WHERE E2.Salary > E1.Salary);
-- top-k with ties (k = 2 lowest): < k strictly better
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE E2
       WHERE E2.Salary < E1.Salary) < 2
-- argmax with ties (largest total): 10 and 30
WITH T AS (SELECT Pno, SUM(Hours) AS Total
           FROM WORKS_ON GROUP BY Pno)
SELECT Pno FROM T WHERE Total = (SELECT MAX(Total) FROM T);
-- subtotals without CUBE (E = EMPLOYEE)
SELECT Dno, Sex, SUM(Salary) FROM E GROUP BY Dno, Sex
UNION ALL SELECT Dno, NULL, SUM(Salary) FROM E GROUP BY Dno
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, Sex, SUM(Salary) FROM E GROUP BY Sex
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, NULL, SUM(Salary) FROM E;
    • 2nd highest: MAX over Salary < (SELECT MAX …). Window forms: DENSE_RANK() = n, RANK() <= k.
    • Argmax also OK: HAVING SUM(Hours) >= ALL (…) (fails if a SUM is NULL). Wrong: LIMIT 1, MAX(SUM()), aggregate in WHERE, a hard-coded value.
    • Subtotals: one GROUP BY per column subset, NULL in rolled-up columns, UNION ALL. ROLLUP = prefixes only.

    Views

    • CREATE VIEW V (c1,c2) AS SELECT …: virtual, always current. Query modification vs materialization (immediate / lazy / periodic).
    • Updatable: single table, no aggregates/grouping, has the PK and every NOT NULL column without default. Not: joins (ambiguous), aggregates (no base meaning).
    • WITH CHECK OPTION: rejects INSERT/UPDATE via the view producing a row failing the view’s WHERE.
    • Update via view = base update with the view’s WHERE added (… WHERE Dno=4 AND Salary>40000); view aggregate conditions become HAVING; deletes hit base rows (FK actions apply).

    Schema change

    • DROP TABLE|SCHEMA x CASCADE (also drops dependents) / RESTRICT (only if unreferenced / empty). DROP removes the definition, DELETE only rows.
    • ALTER TABLE T ADD COLUMN c … (NULL everywhere: NOT NULL needs DEFAULT); DROP COLUMN c CASCADE|RESTRICT; ALTER COLUMN c SET|DROP DEFAULT; ADD|DROP CONSTRAINT name (named only).

    Database programming

    • Embedded SQL (EXEC SQL, precompiler; SQLJ #sql); API (ODBC, JDBC); new language (PL/SQL). Impedance mismatch = type mismatch + set vs record (cursor).
    • Host vars in BEGIN/END DECLARE SECTION, written :v. SQLCODE 0 ok, 100 no data, <0<0<0 error (SQLSTATE ’02000’). SELECT INTO only for one row.
    EXEC SQL DECLARE EMP CURSOR FOR SELECT Ssn, Salary
  FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Dno = :dno FOR UPDATE OF Salary;
EXEC SQL OPEN EMP;                   /* before row 1 */
EXEC SQL FETCH FROM EMP INTO :ssn, :salary;
while (SQLCODE == 0) {
  EXEC SQL UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Salary = Salary + :raise
           WHERE CURRENT OF EMP;
  EXEC SQL FETCH FROM EMP INTO :ssn, :salary; }
EXEC SQL CLOSE EMP;
EXEC SQL PREPARE cmd FROM :sqlstring;   /* dynamic */
EXEC SQL EXECUTE cmd;     /* or EXECUTE IMMEDIATE */

    Traps that cost marks

    • ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 with ties (−2.5/10-2.5/10−2.5/10); = (subquery) returning several rows.
    • “For all” as a plain join (that is “some”); <> join for “not related”; OR for “neither… nor”.
    • Inner join drops unmatched rows; COUNT(*) after LEFT JOIN counts the padded row.
    • NOT IN on a nullable column with no assumption; = NULL; missing join (Cartesian); wrong self-join direction (E.Super_ssn = S.Ssn: S supervises E).
    • SET NULL on a PK/NOT NULL FK; FK actions without reasons; composite FK split.
    • Views: show the modified base query; “not allowed” needs the reason.

    Exam moves

    • Assumptions as SQL comments with reasons (keys, non-NULL FKs, ties, empty groups): a mark per part. Any dialect; slips are free unless rows change.
    • “Write the output”: show the joined rows/groups first; write “empty” with the reason. Joins: inner count, then padded rows.
    • Step questions: one statement per step on the current table; ORDER BY a position column.
